subtopic: EXPRESSIONS OF WELCOME ON RETURN FROM OVERSEAS

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: EXPRESSIONS OF WELCOME ON RETURN FROM OVERSEAS
speechtext:
I am sure all members of the house are glad to see that the Prime Minister's seat is once again occupied by the Prime Minister himself. On behalf of the official opposition I wish to extend to him a cordial welcome back to Canada and to the House of Commons. I am glad to see that he is looking well after his trip. I trust that he has found his trip not only useful but pleasant as well. I may say to him that during his absence we have done our best to keep the government on the straight and narrow path of rectitude, but in that we have been only partly successful. We have saved up a few things for his consideration on his return, among others such minor matters as the budget, redistribution, and so forth. For these reasons I am sure

The Prime Minister
that those who sit at his back will be as glad as we are in the opposition to welcome him home.
As a matter of interest, the Prime Minister returned on a ship which, according to the papers, carried two thousand brides. I would be the last to offer the Prime Minister any advice in his domestic affairs, and I suppose I would be the last from whom he would accept any such advice, but having failed at least in one respect during his threescore years and ten,
I am sure the Canadian people would not have objected had that ship contained two thousand and one brides.
Again let me say on behalf of the official opposition that we cordially welcome the Prime Minister, and we look forward to the report of his visit overseas.

subtopic: EXPRESSIONS OF WELCOME ON RETURN FROM OVERSEAS
speechtext:
It is unnecessary for me to add anything to what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) has said. We join with him in his welcome to the Prime Minister. We are glad to see him back, and for a change we agree with all that the leader of the opposition said.
Mr. SOLON E. LOW (Peace River): May I join with the two hon. gentlemen who have spoken in welcoming the Prime Minister, and say that I have been looking forward to his return ever since he left, because I am still very much concerned about the hot weather. I am happy he is here again, because it augurs well for some speed in getting through the work of the session, so that we shall not have to sit here through the heat of the summer. We are pleased to see him looking so well.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: EXPRESSIONS OF WELCOME ON RETURN FROM OVERSEAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I need
scarcely say I am indeed deeply touched by the welcome extended to me this afternoon on my return from a journey overseas. May I at once thank my hon. friends, the leader of the opposition and the leaders of the other parties who have spoken, for the cordial manner in which they have extended greetings on their own behalf and on behalf of their followers. May I say to the members of my own party, to my colleagues in the government and to our supporters, how delighted I am to be back again helping to share with them in the solution of some of the problems and in helping to bear some of the burdens which they have been carrying exclusively, during the time that I have been away.
I should like to say a word of thanks to the house for giving me the opportunity, which I have had in the last five weeks, of paying a very memorable visit to the old country. The main purpose of the visit hon.
members know was to participate in the proceedings of the conference of prime ministers which had commenced some weeks before I left, but which had been adjourned in order to give me the opportunity of joining with the premiers of the other nations of the commonwealth in reviewing situations and problems of common interest. I found that opportunity of exceptional value.
I shall keep in mind the wish expressed by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) that I should report to the house on the conference at a later and more appropriate stage, but at this moment I should like to express very warmly my appreciation of the many courtesies extended by the government of the United Kingdom, and in particular by the Prime Minister, Mr. Attlee, and the secretary of state for dominion affairs, Lord Addison; also of the courtesies extended by their colleagues, and the facilities that were afforded for gaining first-hand information on imporantant public matters from as many sources as possible during the period of my stay.
My absence covered a period of five weeks. Two weeks were spent in the trip to and fro.
I want to express appreciation of the opportunity that was thereby afforded to get a little rest and, while taking the ocean voyage and having the benefit of the sea air for that length of time, to reflect on many questions which are of real concern to us all. The three weeks in London were necessarily very much occupied with the proceedings of the conference and with consultations with different members of the government. During that period I also had the opportunity of witnessing the marvellous victory parade which took place in that city. That parade I believe will prove a line of demarcation between the past and its associations with war, and the future with its outlook for better conditions for human society. I wish 'all hon. members might have been privileged as I was to witness that parade. From what they have seen in the illustrated papers of views of the mechanized colum, they must realize something of the tremendous power it was necessary for the nations of the commonwealth and allied nations to exert in order to defend freedom and civilization from the enemies who were seeking to overthrow them. Similarly from a view of. the marching column one got a fuller appreciation of the tremendous contribution made by the manhood and womanhood of the different free nations toward victory. It has secured the condition we have in the world to-day which, though still one of unrest, is free from actual war. Looking
The Prime Minister

beneath the surface one could not but feel deeply the tremendous burden mankind seems to have had placed upon its shoulders in the recent past, and could not but wonder what will happen to human society if soon we do not find some way of effecting peace and good will among the nations of the world.
I should like to say a special word about the place our contingents, of the navy, the army and the air force, held in that memorable procession on the occasion of the victory parade. The Canadian contingents were recognized immediately by the multitudes along the streets and were given a wonderful reception. I was never in my life prouder of being a citizen of Canada than as I witnessed that parade, and reflected upon the position which Canada holds in the eyes of other nations as a result of the great part our defence forces have played in preserving the liberty of the world. May I add that I was never more grateful that this country is a member of the great community of nations which constitutes the British commonwealth and empire than I am at this moment, as a result of what I have seen and learned in a more intimate way in the course of this last visit. This is a time when all of us who love freedom cannot be bound together too closely by every possible bond that will cement relations between nations; and we are fortunate indeed in belonging to a great community of free nations which, in free combination with the powerful forces of the United States, have done and will, I believe, continue to do more to preserve freedom than would be possible in any other way.
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, that on the way overseas or coming back I was not able to improve the opportunity along the lines suggested by my hon. friend, the leader of the opposition. But may I say that while I believe threescore years and ten are something of a handicap, I have not yet lost hope that there may be opportunities of happiness for myself and others, which he apparently so greatly desires should be mine.
I was deeply impressed while away by what I learned of the very serious condition of the world at the present time. It may seem a commonplace in the light of what has been stated from various sources to say it, but one could not participate in conferences such as we had, or have the privilege as was mine of conversing with those who have inside knowledge of the situation, without realizing that at this moment the situation in the world is in some respects as difficult as it has been at any time in history. In England, to appearances
fMr. Mackenzie King.]
at least, there has been some improvement. Outwardly at least the people look better; there is a note of hope, and a happier expression on their countenances. But they know that all the fortitude which was required during the war is still required to carry them through the situation facing them at the present time, and anything that can be done on this side I know will be appreciated over there more than words can express.
May I add that it does seem to me conditions in central Europe are deteriorating rapidly and greatly. Undoubtedly conditions are better in Holland, Denmark and Belgium, but they are still very difficult in France and are terrible in parts of Germany. Unless some means can be found whereby the new world, and countries that have supplies of food and clothing, can furnish those supplies to the people of some of the occupied zones and other parts of Europe, there may be conditions of famine, of strife and of turmoil which will amount to something in the nature of the spread of a new revolution throughout Europe. I think I am not wrong in giving that as an impression-not from what I have seen in Europe, because unfortunately I did not have the chance ito pay the personal visit that I had hoped I might, but from what I have gathered from those who have inside information.
The last word I should like to say at the moment is that, as far as one can judge what will go farther than anything else in helping to meet present world conditions is increased production and more effective distribution. The need in Europe to-day is to get industry under way, to get people at work. There is the prospect of a good harvest, but in some areas it has been impossible thus far to find any means whereby large numbers who should be employed can be given work, because of lack of fuel, food and transportation. Anything that can be done in the world to-day to furnish the necessities of life to those parts of Europe which are in dire need will not only mean salvation for them, but may well be in the nature of salvation for the world as a whole.
Third report of the standing committee on standing orders.-Mr. MacLean.

subtopic: * ACQUISITION OF MANITOBA RAILWAY

speechtext:
Hon. LIONEL CHEVRIER (Minister of Transport) moved for leave to introduce bill No. 194, respecting Canadian National Railways and the acquisition of the Manitoba Railway.

Questions
He said: Mr. Speaker, by virtue of this bill the Canadian National Railways seeks authority from the house to purchase the Manitoba Railway. The Manitoba Railway is an amalgamation of The Northern Pacific and Manitoba Railway company, the Winnipeg Transfer Railway company, the Portage and Northwestern Railway company and the Waskada and Northeastern Railway company. In the year 1901 these railway companies, the names of which I have just mentioned, leased to the crown in the right of the province of Manitoba their railways and undertaking, for a period of 999 years. The lease was afterwards assigned by the province of Manitoba to the Canadian Northern Railway company; and the Canadian Northern Railway company is part of the Canadian National Railways. One of the terms of the lease referred to in 1901 provided for payment of an annual rental of $300,000 per year. That has been paid by the Canadian National Railways, since its purchase of the assignment of the lease.
The lease also contained an option to purchase the railway for $7 million, and the Canadian National Railways now seek the right, by virtue of the assignment of the lease, to purchase the railway at the price mentioned. This purchase will mean a substantial saving to the Canadian National Railways, and a consequent reduction in its fixed charges. The committee on railways and shipping, in its consideration of the 1946 budget of the Canadian National Railways, approved the expenditure of this money.

speechtext:
1.	Was any recent request received by the government or any officer thereof, from any person or persons in Toronto, or from the municipal authorities there, regarding the operation of coal, grain and marine shipping on the great lakes and St. Lawrence river, to aid the domestic fuel and grain situation?
2.	If so, from whom; when and to whom was it addressed, and what was the text thereof?
3.	Was any reply given thereto by the government or any officer thereof? If so, by whom?

subtopic: GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext:
1.	Yes.
2.	From His Worship Mayor R. H. Saunders, addressed to the Minister of Labour on June 7. The text of Mayor Saunders telegram was as follows:
"In my opinion a national emergency is being created by the seamen's strike. For the last 24 hours I haim endeavoured to communicate with Alderman Ferguson, vice-president of the seamen's union, seeking his cooperation to have the grain and coal boats operate. As you know, prior to the strike, there was already a grave situation with regard to the shortage of coal. This is, of course, becoming increasingly serious and presents a dangerous situation for the people of this and other cities throughout the dominion and next winter.
Last year, 1,735,000 tons were delivered to this city by ship, of which 418,849 tons arrived prior to June 6, 1945. My information is that so far this year we have received only 97,440 tons. I am further advised that scores of thousands of tons are waiting to be placed on the boats. I am also informed there is no way in which the shortage to date can be made up.
Realizing these conditions and looking forward to extreme difficulty the coming winter season for the people whom I represent I ask most emphatically that our government take oirer and operate the ships carrying grain and coal so that our people will be assured of at least some protection during the coming months and particularly during next winter.
I would be pleased with an immediate reply."
3.	Yes; on June 8 and June 11 by the Minister of Labour.

*Foreign Exchange Control

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATUTORY AUTHORITY FOR ORDERS IN COUNCIL PASSED UNDER WAR MEASURES ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the purpose of this legislation is to provide for the continuance of foreign exchange control. As the committee is aware, exchange control has been in operation in Canada since September 15, 1939, having been introduced by virtue of an order in council passed under the provisions of the War Measures Act.
In asking the committee to approve legislation to continue exchange control, I have felt that I should tell the war-time story of exchange operations and that the committee should have certain information which, for security reasons, was withheld during the war. I have tabled a report of the foreign exchange control board which gives full details and I propose, in introducing this measure, to touch on the high spots of the happenings in this field during the war years. I shall be prepared to make detailed explanations of the various provisions of the bill before the committee at a later stage of the proceedings.
I should like to begin by reminding the committee of the reasons for the original decision to impose exchange control. We were, at the outbreak of war, one of the world's largest debtor countries. One of our main preoccupations was consequently the fear that our international debtor status might interfere with an all-out effort on the economic front-in other words, that exchange shortages, in particular a shortage of United States dollars, might become a bottleneck in the Canadian war effort.
There were three main dangers involved in the situation. First, there was the danger of fluctuations in the exchange rate, with unsettling effects on commodity prices and on business generally. Second, there was the danger that foreign holdings of Canadian securities would be dumped on the Canadian market and the proceeds withdrawn from the country in U.S. dollars with the result that we would be left with insufficient supplies of foreign exchange to cover our war requirements and to meet our normal current and capital obligations as they fell due. Finally, the panicky sale of securities in our market would have been highly detrimental to an orderly programme of war financing. In this respect, the main danger lay, of course, in the very large amounts of our securities held by residents of the United States, at that time a neutral country.
I wish to refer in somewhat greater detail to the anticipated scarcity of U.S. dollars. For some years before the outbreak of war, Canada's international receipts and payments on current account had resulted in a credit balance. Our current receipts of foreign exchange from the export of goods and services
CMr. Coldwell.]
and from the production of newly-mined gold exceeded our current payments abroad for imports, interest and dividends on the foreign investment in Canada and other invisible items. This surplus on our current account transactions went, of course, towards improving our international capital position-we were making a start at reducing our large balance of international indebtedness.
The over-all surplus on our current account transactions with the rest of the world in the years just before the outbreak of war was made up, however, of two main elements which are clearly shown in the table on page 6 of the foreign exchange control board report which has been tabled. The United Kingdom was our most important market while the United States was our most important supplier. With the United Kingdom, the rest of the sterling area, and with the continent of Europe, we had a surplus; with the United States we had a deficit. We had to expect that wartime conditions would aggravate the situation in two ways. On the one hand, our deficit with the United States was certain to increase since many of the things required in the war production programme were imported from that country. On the other hand, although our surplus with the United Kingdom was expected to increase as a result of increased shipments from Canada, this surplus would no longer be freely convertible into United States funds in view of the necessary establishment of exchange control by the United Kingdom.
In these circumstances it was clear that we would be hard put to make both ends meet so far as U.S. dollars were concerned and that it would be necessary to supervise all foreign exchange transactions to ensure that the pressure on our U.S. dollar resources was not aggravated as a result of capital withdrawals by non-residents or capital flight by residents. In a statement issued at the time exchange control was imposed, my predecessor, Colonel Ralston, explained that the government had decided that a policy of foreign exchange control was essential to the successful organization of Canada's wartime activities, and that it was necessary during the war to make sure that the country's foreign exchange resources were used in the national interest. He went on to say that the use of Canadian monetary resources for speculation abroad or for other purposes which could not be regarded as necessary or desirable would be bound to hamper Canada's war effort, and should therefore be prevented.

Foreign Exchange Control
Accordingly, the foreign exchange control order placed in the hands of a board responsible to the Minister of Finance control over all financial transactions between residents of Canada and residents of other countries. The board centralizes the foreign exchange resources of the country and is responsible for seeing that foreign exchange earned as a result of exports, etc. becomes available for the general use of the Canadian economy and that foreign exchange is used only for approved purposes. To discharge this responsibility all international transactions involving more than nominal amounts are brought to the board's attention through a system of permits. The only transactions which are restricted, however, are certain transactions involving the export of capital, such as the sale of securities in Canada by non-residents, and the purchase of U.S. funds by residents for the purpose of acquiring securities or otherwise transferring their capital abroad.
Subject to direction by the Minister of Finance, the foreign exchange control board fixes the rates of exchange for the currencies in which it deals. The board's buying rates for U.S. dollars and sterling have remained completely stable at SI.10 and $4.43 respectively since the beginning of exchange control. The selling rates for these currencies, originally $1.11 and $4.47 respectively, were reduced to $1.10| and $4.45 last October. I believe that the house will agree that the complete stability of exchange rates which has been maintained since September 1939 has been of great advantage to the Canadian economy. As I shall show later, the swings in the exchange position have been very considerable and if the exchange rate had been left at the mercy of the temporary oscillations of supply and demand it would, I believe, have undergone quite wide and frequent fluctuations.
Although the exchange control had to be comprehensive in order to be effective, I think it is the general view that it has operated with considerable smoothness. Of one thing I am certain, and that is that the board has made the most conscientious effort to exercise its wide powers with prudence and restraint and to avoid giving cause for complaint that its actions were in any sense arbitrary in character or that they imposed unnecessary formalities on the Canadian public.
The early fears regarding shortage of US. dollars which led to the imposition of exchange control turned out to be fully warranted. True, for the first seven or eight months we were not subject to particularly strong pressure on our U.S. dollar reserves. There was an
adverse balance during this period, but it was largely met out of the gold and U.S. dollars received from the United Kingdom in partial settlement of their deficiency with us. This initial lull provided a welcome opportunity to improve the machinery of exchange control and to explain the necessity* for this control to those affected by it so that their cooperation in observing the provisions of the order might be ensured.
The serious pressure on our U. S. dollar reserves developed when Canadian war production got into its stride. When it became apparent that a heavy drain on our U.S. dollar resources was developing, the government passed an order in council on May 1, 1940, the so-called foreign exchange acquisition order, directing that all foreign exchange held by private individuals and corporations should be offered for sale to the foreign exchange control board. By a separate order in council the Bank of Canada was directed to sell to the foreign exchange control board all gold held in unrestricted ownership, and was relieved of its obligation under the Bank of Canada Act to maintain any minimum reserve ratio of gold or foreign exchange to its sight liabilities. Through these measures all the liquid foreign exchange resources of the country, apart from minimum balances needed for the day-to-day conduct of business operations, were concentrated in official hands. The foreign exchange control board took over from the Bank of Canada gold to a U.S. dollar value of $205 million and U.S. dollar balances amounting to $25 million. Privately held U.S. dollars amounting to $57 million were also taken over; this followed on earlier negotiated transfers of U.S. funds from private to official holdings to an amount exceeding $20 million.
The development of our military production programme after Dunkirk necessarily involved heavy expenditures in the United States for machine tools, other capital equipment, aircraft and military equipment and materials and component parts. In addition, the expansion of incomes in Canada led to increased imports of civilian goods. Our dollar earnings failed by far to keep pace with this increase in our dollar expenditures. Exports to the United States increased appreciably but the overrunning of Europe meant the loss of dollar markets and American tourist expenditures in Canada shrank appreciably in 1940.
To help meet the position, a series of exchange conservation measures were taken in 1940. In the budget of that year a war exchange tax of 10 per cent was imposed on all imports from non-sterling area countries. In July 1940 a complete prohibition was imposed on the use of our US. dollar resources
Foreign Exchange Control

for pleasure travel in the United States. In December 1940 the War Exchange Conservation Act prohibited the import of a long list of non-essential goods from non-sterling area countries and placed others under import quota. These measures saved considerable quantities of exchange in the aggregate-under the conditions prevailing when they were imposed the annual rate of saving may well have exceeded 1150 million. In addition the foreign exchange control board exercised a great deal of ingenuity in devising many ways and means of economizing on U.S. dollar payments and adding to U.S. dollar receipts without interfering with the legitimate business operations of the country.
These steps were, however, not sufficient to stop the drain on our reserves. As the table on page 20 of the report shows, official gold and U.S. dollar reserves, which had already fallen by $72 million in 1940 notwithstanding the receipt of $225 million from the United Kingdom in that year, fell in 1941 from $332 million to $188 million. In the four months ending January 1942 we lost $85 million in reserves. If this rate of loss had continued, our reserves would have been exhausted in a matter of months. Moreover, if it had not been for the special measures of exchange conservation taken in 1940, we would already have been at the bottom of the barrel by the end of 1941. I hope that those who were inconvenienced by the travel restrictions and who co-operated so admirably with the foreign exchange control board at a time when the explanations of the exchange position had, for security reasons, to be general in character, will now be assured that these restrictions were an important factor enabling us to keep our heads above water.
The situation was indeed a serious one in 1941. We had mobilized all our privately-held reserves and had received from the United Kingdom gold and U.S. dollar payments in partial settlement of their deficit with us to an amount of $225 million in terms of U.S. funds-as much as they could afford. These extraordinary accretions to our reserves had been spent and our remaining reserves in gold and U.S. dollars were much below any figure that could reasonably be regarded as the minimum working balances of a country with Canada's volume of international transactions. In spite of the measures of exchange conservation taken, we were running a current account deficit in our transactions with the United States at the rate of some $300 million per year.
New sources of receipts of U.S. dollars were clearly necessary if Canada was to continue to purchase the great variety of United States

commodities required for the prosecution of the war. The United States introduced the lend-lease programme in 1941, but Canada never wished to ask the United States for lend-lease assistance. We felt, as I have said in the house on a previous occasion, that as a nation in a favoured position, free from the ravages of war, we were in duty bound to stand on our own feet and, indeed, to share with the United States in assisting other less fortunate of our allies in carrying on the war against the common enemy.
A means of providing Canada with new sources of dollars to finance part of our war purchases in the United States, while at the same time mobilizing the resources of the continent most effectively for the production of war goods, was found in that most statesmanlike arrangement made by our Prime Minister and the President of the United States in April, 1941, and generally known as the Hyde Park declaration. It was agreed in this declaration that "each country should provide the other with the defence articles which it is best able to produce, and above all, produce quickly, and that production programmes should be coordinated to that end." Canada's purchases of war goods in the United States were already very heavy and increasing; under this agreement the United States undertook to increase its purchases in Canada of urgently needed war supplies in respect of which we had facilities for speedy and economical production.
Receipts of U.S. exchange by War Supplies limited, the company which was organized to handle the sales of munitions, ships and other war supplies under the Hyde Park agreement, amounted to $275 million in 1942, $301 million in 1943 and $314 million in 1944. These figures are net, after making allowance for price adjustments and repayment of advances in the later years.
I should like to place on record my conviction that the Hyde Park agreement and the spirit which prompted its conception and guided its execution constitute an outstanding example of the neighbourly goodwill and capacity for constructive cooperation which is so often found in our dealings with the United States. Like all good bargains, this was one from which both sides gained advantages. We were given, at a time when the outlook was darkest, the assurance that a shortage of U.S. exchange would not impede our war effort-that we would be able to go on getting the war goods we needed in the United States by producing war goods which the United

Foreign Exchange Control
States needed. The United States, for its part, got full value in the form of vital munitions of war.
In essence, what the Hyde Park arrangements involved was an exchange of war goods between Canada and the United States in accordance with the character and availability of productive capacity. In the aggregate, of course, our purchases of war goods from the United States were considerably higher than our sales of war goods to them. Net sales through War Supplies Limited amounted, as I have indicated already, to approximately SS90 million to the end of 1944. From the start of the war until the end of 1945, imports of goods purchased by Canada from the United States amounted to over $6,000 million and it is estimated that the war content of our imports was about half this sum.
Notwithstanding these very large outlays we made on the purchase of war supplies in the United States, certain unexpected developments to which I shall refer in a moment resulted in additions to our cash resources in gold and U.S. dollars during the period when large contracts were being placed by agencies of the United States government with War Supplies Limited. It was not the desire of either the Canadian or the United States government that the operation of the Hyde Park agreement should have the effect, or even appear to have the effect, of building up Canada's liquid balances in U.S. funds just as it was not the desire of either government to let them fall too low. Accordingly, when it was found that our balances were rising as a result of the factors to which I shall refer, the Canadian government in pursuance of previous agreement with the United States government, offset this tendency by making certain payments to the United States treasury in the
spring of 1944. I informed the house regarding the nature of these transactions on April 21, 1944.
The unexpected developments leading to an improvement in our U.S. dollar position in the course of 1942, 1943 and 1944 were three in number-sales of securities in the United States, United States government expenditures in Canada, and unusually large sales of grain to the United States.
United States interest in Canadian securities developed on a large scale in 1942 and persisted in later years. In addition, Canadian sales of Canadian held United States securities brought in appreciable amounts of U.S. exchange. The net proceeds of security sales exceeded $100 million in each of the years 1942 to 1944 and exceeded $250 million in 1945. United States government expenditures in Canada in connection with the Alaska highway and other government projects are estimated to have averaged over $80 million in these years, reaching their peak in 1943.
Finally, the extraordinary sales of wheat and coarse grains to the United States brought in approximately $150 million in 1943 and nearly $300 million in 1944. The latter figure is only slightly below our total exports of all commodities to the United States in 1939. In 1945 receipts from this source were in the neighbourhood of $100 million.
The committee will appreciate that receipts of exchange from the last two sources were of a fortuitous and non-recurring character while receipts from security sales do not cause any change in our over-all international financial position. It has been the determination of the people of this country that financial considerations should not impede or delay the victory by limiting the arms and other supplies that we put into the common pool. It was also their desire that our contribution of supplies should not result in international indebtedness on a scale that would be burdensome to international commerce.

Total sterling area expenditures during these years amounted to approximately $11,000 million. This left an aggregate deficiency after Canadian military expenditures of nearly $6,000 million. It was financed to the extent of $700 million by official repatriation of securities, to the extent of $340 million by private repatriation of securi-63260-161i
ties, to the extent of $500 million by the sale of gold and U.S. dollars to Canada, to the extent of $560 million net (after allowing for the application of the proceeds of sales of Canadian securities by residents of the United Kingdom on the original amount of $700 million) by the interest-free Canadian dollar loan, to the extent of $1,000 million by the gift of 1942 and to the extent of $2,175 by mutual aid.
So much by way of summary of our wartime financial relationships with the U.S. dollar area and with the sterling area. We have, as the committee will see, been through some difficult moments and have had to face problems of enormous magnitude. I think that we are entitled to feel that we have done reasonably well in handling these problems.. Hon. members will recall my statement of the dangers we saw originally which led to the imposition of exchange control-the danger-
Foreign Exchange Control

of a fluctuating exchange rate, the danger of large non-resident sales of securities on our markets, the danger of a shortage of U.S dollars leading to a contraction of our war effort. We have fared well on all these scores. The exchange rate has been kept completely stable since September 15, 1939; we have not added the further uncertainty of a fluctuating exchange rate to the inevitable uncertainties of -war. Canadian credit abroad stands higher than ever before. And we have met all our obligations in U.S. funds and are in a relatively strong cash position. The operation of the exchange control has been an important, indeed an indispensable factor, in producing these results.
The relatively strong cash position to which I have referred enables us to face the future with a greater degree of confidence than would otherwise have been possible. Since the end of the war our imports from the United States have continued to run at very high levels and it is reasonable to expect that in reequipping our industry we shall have to import many goods which have not been available, or only in inadequate quantities, during the war. Moreover, it is to be expected that the high level of incomes in Canada will lead, as it has done in the past, to increased imports of civilian goods, particularly consumers' durable goods, as they again become available in quantity. On the other hand, the special exports of war supplies and of grain to the United States which, as I have shown, figured so largely on the income side of dollar exchange during the past years, have fallen away. Our current account with the United States, which was about in balance for some time, is again showing a deficit. In the first quarter of this year the loss of United States funds from current account transactions (excluding collections on past business effected by War Supplies Limited) amounted to $50 million. The fact that we hold sizeable cash reserves means that we can face any deficit which it is now reasonable to anticipate without having to consider taking restrictive measures to eliminate it. It does not, however, mean that we can throw overboard all control over our exchange resources. In addition to the current account deficit with the United States which is now developing, we must naturally stand ready to meet all our capital obligations as they fall due. During the next 12 years Canadian bonds and debentures payable solely or optionally in U.S. dollars fall due in an amount of $1,000 million, the bulk of which is held in the United States. Of this total, some $400. million represents dominion, dominion-guaranteed and C.N.R. issues. Here, too, I hasten to say that we have no doubt that our cash reserves

and prospects are such that we shall be well able to meet both these capital payments and the current account deficits I have referred to. But we feel that we cannot, as well, undertake the obligation which would be inherent in a decision to do away with exchange control to find U.S. exchange for non-residents who wish to sell securities on the Canadian market and withdraw their capital from Canada or for residents who, without valid reason, may wish to transfer their capital abroad. The exchange resources of the country must be at the disposal of the national economy and must not be dissipated through capital flight.
In reaching the conclusion I have stated, the government was naturally influenced by the uncertainties of the world outlook. In our view, these are so great that a country in Canada's position has no real choice but to continue to control exchange transactions. In introducing the Bretton Woods Agreement Act last December I dwelt at some length on those uncertainties and need therefore allude to them only briefly here. No one can say at the present time what will be the character of the economic system which emerges in the world as the war-devastated areas reconstruct their own shattered internal economic structures. We shall either go forward to a degree of co-operation among countries with regard to international trade and financial matters which is greater than anything we have known in the recent past or we shall enter a period of intense international economic rivalry and discord. The Canadian interest is so bound up with the expansion of world trade and with liberal economic relationships among nations that we must clearly throw our whole weight in favour of the first alternative. This we have been doing in every way open to us, and most recently by the decision of this house to have Canada join the two Bretton Woods institutions and to extend large credits to the United Kingdom and other countries.
Through these positive steps Canada has demonstrated its willingness to make its constructive contribution to solving the economic problems confronting the world This does not mean however, that we can afford to throw all caution to the winds and act as though the world's economic problems had been solved. For some time to come the international financial situation of many countries will continue to be abnormal and we shall have to count on providing a large portion of our exports to certain of these countries on credit terms. These exports will not produce equivalent amounts of foreign exchange which we shall

Foreign Exchange Control
be able to use to pay for our imports from the United States. We are therefore thrown back on the necessity of being in a position to control any undesirable drain on our U.S. dollar reserves, and in view of the very large amount of Canadian securites held by non-residents it is particularly necessary to be able to guard against the pressure of capital withdrawals from Canada. I have already informed the house that during the past few years the pressure has been in the other direction and that we have gained exchange and not lost it as a result of nonresident transactions in Canadian securities. I have no reason for believing that this trend will be reversed in the near future. But I am also awrare that rapid changes have taken place in the past, both in our exchange position and in the attitude of non-residents towards Canadian securities. At present there is a keen interest on the part of American investors in Canadian securities, but I consider it my duty not to forget that there have been times during the recent war when Canada's premier securities sold in the American market on a 7 and 8 per cent yield basis, and were quoted at a price 40 per cent below the valuation placed on similar securities by the more confident Canadian public. In the light of such disturbing volatility, we cannot base our long-term policies on the favourable attitude towards Canadian securities in evidence at this particular moment or count on the indefinite continuance of that attitude.
The control of foreign exchange transactions which this legislation contemplates will provide the machinery for discharging certain of the obligations assumed by Canada in becoming a member of the international monetary fund. Under the fund agreement "each member undertakes to collaborate with the fund to promote exchange stability, to maintain orderly exchange arrangements with other members and to avoid competitive exchange depreciation" (Articles of agreement of international monetary fund, article IV, section 4 (a)). There are three possible methods of discharging this obligation. One would be to return to the international gold standard and make the Canadian dollar convertible into gold at a fixed price. I am not prepared to advise the house to adopt this course. The second would be to operate an exchange equalization account which would intervene in the exchange market by buying or selling foreign exchange in order to maintain exchange rates at whatever level had been determined, but which would exercise no qualitative supervision over exchange transactions. The third
method, and the one we have chosen, is to operate an exchange control which will buy and sell foreign exchange at fixed rates but which will exercise a qualitative supervision over exchange transactions to ensure that any involving capital flight which are contrary to the national interest are prohibited. The fund agreement clearly contemplates that certain countries will continue to operate exchange controls after joining since it provides in article VI, section 3, that "members may exercise such controls as are necessary to regulate international capital movements."
I should like to summarize what I have said in this way. The general character of the international financial and economic relations between nations which is going to prevail in the future is still uncertain. We hope that it will be one which does not call for restrictive controls and we shall do everything in-our power to bring this about. But we cannot be certain that the world we are going into will be what we would like to see. It may be a world of economic friction instead of cooperation. Canada is in an exposed international position, on account of our international debtor status and on account of the great importance of international transactions in our economic life. WTe cannot demobilize our main economic defence without being absolutely certain that it will not be needed. We cannot leave ourselves in a position where our choice of domestic economic policies has to be influenced by the consideration that one policy or another may lead to capital withdrawal by foreigners or capital flight by Canadians.
We have no intention of using this exchange control legislation to restrict anything but certain types of capital movement. We expect to be able to avoid any interference with current account transactions. But experience, both our own and other peoples', has shown that to control capital movements effectively it is necessary to supervise all transactions between residents and non-residents. Let me give one illustration of this point. If we attempted to control capital exports merely by refusing to sell foreign exchange for this purpose, it would be open to anyone who wished to export his capital illegally to say that he required the exchange to pay for imports. Similarly, anyone could buy goods in Canada and export them without bringing the exchange proceeds back home. In either case a transaction which appears to be quite innocent on the surface is in fact an export of capital. It is for this reason that it is necessary to maintain our over-all machinery
Foreign Exchange Control

of control even though our intention is to place no restrictions on current account transactions.
I believe that there has been general appreciation during the war years of the benefits of exchange stability, and that the business community will welcome the assurance provided by this measure that the government intends, through the continuance of exchange control, to guard against a return to the situation that prevailed in this respect after the last war. Some members may recall the difficulties and hardships caused by the wide fluctuation in the price of sterling and U.S. funds in Canada in the past. Between 1919 and 1920 the United States dollar fluctuated between If per cent premium and 19J per cent premium in Canada. Again in 1933 it moved within a range of 11 per cent discount to 23 per cent premium. Sharp fluctuations of this sort are injurious to business anjl of advantage only to the exchange speculator. We do not wish to return to this situation. We want those engaged in international transactions to have some assurance that they will not be faced with arbitrary and erratic fluctuations in exchange rates that upset their price calculations and turn profits into losses.
I realize that the machinery of control is not without its burdens to those engaged in foreign transactions and I hope that this section of the community will understand the necessity of continuing the control. The foreign exchange control board has tried to reduce its formalities to the minimum compatible with effective control and I am sure that it will continue to make further efforts in this direction. I.should like at this point to pay a tribute to the business community for the way in which they have cooperated with the foreign exchange control board during the war. I should also like to express appreciation to the public generally for its cooperation, particularly in accepting with such good grace the unpalatable but necessary travel restrictions. When the reasons for the control measures were explained and understood, the business community and the public generally were at all times willing to assist the board in carrying them out. I must also make a special reference to the chartered banks who have acted as agents of the exchange control authorities. Exchange control necessarily involved considerable additional work for them. This work has been carried out in a very satisfactory manner and they have at all times given their full cooperation to the control authorities.
In conclusion, I wish to assure the committee, if such assurance is needed, that the
[Mr. Ilsley.l
government's decision to maintain exchange control is not due to any fondness for controls as such. When the world returns to a more normal basis we shall have a fresh look at the question. Meanwhile, world conditions are far from normal and we cannot act as though they are. With the exception of the United States, practically every country in the world has exchange control and expects to continue it at least for the transition period. This being the case, Canada has no satisfactory alternative but to retain its control and operate it on the most liberal possible basis.

subtopic: STATUTORY AUTHORITY FOR ORDERS IN COUNCIL PASSED UNDER WAR MEASURES ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of forgetting the convenient arrangement which has been suggested for dealing with this measure, and at this time I wish to make only one or two brief observations.
I venture to suggest to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) that this measure is of such importance and will have so many technical aspects that he might very well allow a good many days before having it brought forward for full discussion. That however is a matter for his consideration.
I should like to make only a few observations respecting the situation in which we find ourselves. Speaking for myself, I do not see how anyone can dissent from the minister in his description of the world of to-day. I remember when we were debating Bretton Woods in this house about six months ago the statement was made by several hon. members that international relations had deteriorated lamentably within the preceding six months. Particularly in view of what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said this afternoon, I think we shall find it hard to believe that they have not deteriorated still further in the interval. That raises the problems which the minister has described, and I doubt if any one will be able to avoid the conclusion he has reached, that some measure of control is necessary. For how long, we do not know.
I want to make just one comment on that. We have heard described this afternoon a technical job well done. I do not think there will be any grudging of credit for what has been done. I think we all feel that it has been done well.
It is obvious to say that people who have done a good job well, who have been in the position of controlling and really making the financial system tick for several years, would be inhuman if they did not somehow believe that they could go on and make it tick indefinitely.
The minister has spoken about a possibility -one does not like even to hear the words-

Foreign Exchange Control
of a period of intense economic rivalry, and then he went on to say that we must be absolutely certain-I have forgotten his exact words, but this is their effect-of our security before we let these things down. It is on that that I would like to say a word. If we are all going to make sure that we get our own security, that is the surest way of making certain that there will be no security. I agree with the minister when he says that we have to use caution; nevertheless it seems to me that if everybody uses caution, if everybody is the last to show any courage and to become cooperative, the results will not be what we want. I am sure that is not the minister's intention. From what has been said in this house by the minister and by others I am sure he will agree with what I have just said.
I should like to leave that with the committee and with the minister. He has given us this afternoon a description of a world which can easily degenerate into suspicious and economic rivalries and exclusiveness such as we had in the nineteen thirties. It seems to me that that should make us aware of our serious responsibilities in arriving at the decisions at which we must arrive. Although it is only economic danger, that faces us at the moment, I am reminded of a line from Shakespeare:
. . . We are in great danger;-[DOT]
Economic danger.
The greater therefore should our courage be.

subtopic: STATUTORY AUTHORITY FOR ORDERS IN COUNCIL PASSED UNDER WAR MEASURES ACT
speechtext:
I have one word to say and one question to ask the minister. The statement just made by the minister was an important one, and I think it is a little hard for the ordinary member of parliament fully to understand foreign exchange and high finance control. A thought that enters my mind has to do with the position of Great Britain and the United States with regard to trade with Canada. Great Britain buys more goods from Canada than we buy from her, and yet the pound is down to $4.38 which means that she gets less for the pound she expends in Canada than does the United States, where conditions are exactly the reverse. We in this country buy more from the United States than they do from us. I have always wondered in my own mind who actually sets the differential in exchange. We would seem to have made a contribution of $600 million to the United States since the war began in the form of the ten per cent exchange, that is, the United States dollar being worth $1.10 Canadian. The opposite is the case with Great Britain. I would have thought that in this new world that we are fashioning the very opposite condition would have prevailed.
I would have thought that in poorer countries like Great Britain it would be made more possible to buy more with their currencies, and that at least the Canadian dollar would be equal to the United States dollar. During the past three years I have asked the Minister of Finance the question: Who sets this differentiation in exchange between the Canadian and United States dollars? It may be my fault, but I do not think I have had a proper explanation. I trust the committee when the bill is before it will go into the two points I have mentioned.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am going to avail myself for a moment of the prerogative which the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) mentioned a moment ago of discussing an important matter on the motion to go into supply. I hesitate to take up the time of the house, but the question I am going to raise is of the utmost importance.
But first on the point raised by the leader of the opposition I think it would be quite in order for the government to move one of the departments into supply because I realize that the government must have a certain amount of manoeuvrability. The only thing I am afraid of is that they will manoeuvre too much. If we could only be sure that

Supply-Labour Conditions
they would not do that I would have no objection to one new department going into supply because the government must have something to put before the house on Thursdays and Fridays.
I hesitated about bringing up the matter, to which I am about to refer, although not to the point of not referring to it at all. I hesitated until I heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) this afternoon refer to the terrible condition, the dangerous condition that prevails in Europe. If there is a dangerous condition in Europe we cannot hope in the small world in which we live to-day to avoid that danger any more than we could in 1939.
There are at the present time a number of labour disputes in progress in the country which are retarding production. I think there is no member of the house, regardless of where he sits, who will not agree with me that the greatest need of the world to-day is production, and that we should all do everything we can to see that production is not retarded. I have already referred to this need in different words on two or three different occasions this session. I referred to it in my speech on the address on March 22, when I urged that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) or some other minister of the government should call a conference of representatives of employers, representatives of organized labour and representatives of the provincial governments in order that we might come to some understanding and some conclusions in regard to the need for increased production. After that was done, the attention of the public could be drawn, as was so often done during the war, to the dangerous position that we and the world are in. We could .then get the cooperation of the public in the same way as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) mentioned this afternoon we got it so often in other matters.
There is a shipping strike-a disastrous strike, in my opinion- and the Minister of Labour has worked hard, I believe, to bring it to a satisfactory conclusion. It being a matter affecting navigation, I believe it comes wholly within the jurisdiction of the federal department of labour. Last Thursday the Minister of Labcur brought together representatives of the shipping companies and representatives of the union concerned and presented them with a formula for the settlement of the strike. I am informed by the president of the seamen's union that it w^as immediately accepted by the union. According to a news report in the Ottawa Journal of June 14. the shipping companies decided that they would take the minister's proposals 63260-162
under consideration the following day. Then, according to the same report, they decided that they would not discuss them until Monday, that is to-day; and later on it was decided that they will not discuss them until tomorrow. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that no matter what the grievance may be this lackadaisical manner of dealing with so urgent a matter should not be tolerated at a time like this. The government have an obligation to the people of Canada, who also are partners in these matters, because to-day there is no labour dispute in which there are not at least three	parties-the employers, the
workers, and the community-and the government must act for the community. I believe that the government has an obligation to-day to secure a quick decision from the shipping companies. It should ask them whether or not they are going to accept the formula proposed by the Minister of Labour, and if they will not act the government should see to it that shipping moves again.
On the west coast, in the lumber situation, we have the opposite condition. The employers have accepted the commissioner's proposals of settlement and the labour organization concerned has rejected them. Here again the government has an obligation to prevent as far as it possibly can the wastage of food and to get into operation as many lumber mills as it is within its power to do, in order to meet the urgent needs of the fruit growers.
There are other disputes. Last Thursday or Friday I brought to the attention of the Minister of Labour a dispute in British Columbia in which the moulders are concerned. I believe the moulders' organization is the union involved in the strike. But the strike is affecting a large number of plants which, I am told have no concern at all with the strike. I am informed by one of the companies that when they took this matter up with the government of British Columbia they were told that the administration of the labour relations regulations came under the federal government; but when I drew this matter to the atention of the Minister of Labour here the other day, and asked if that was a correct statement, he told me that it is wholly in the control of the provincial department of labour. Having so much experience with these regulations. I think this sort of buck-passing should be impossible. I am sorry I have not the communication which I referred to with me: I thought I had and I was going to read from the letter the definite statement that the company had the opinion before-mentioned from the premier of British Columbia.

In my view the minister has been long-suffering in these disputes; he has tried to negotiate fairly between the parties; the formula which he proposed in the seamen's strike is-as far as I know; I am not in a position to judge-a fair one. He should now see to it that the parties concerned get together, and if they do not, the government should take the necessary action in order that goods will float again on the rivers and lakes of this country.

speechtext: -COST OF LIVING

Mr. Speaker, if there is now an opportunity to speak on the labour situation I shall take a few minutes of your time. I want to try again to impress upon the government, and particularly on the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), through you, Mr. Speaker, that in view of w'hat the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said to-day, in my opinion they have even more responsibility on their shoulders than they have apparently realized up to the present time, as far as labour is concerned. I have been negotiating to the best of my ability for the last two weeks with the labour representatives, with a view to getting the box and cooperage factories reopened; I am not speaking of the lumber situation generally. As I understood the Minister of Labour, the union had agreed to man these plants, without prejudice to either side, exactly on the lines of the appeal made by the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Ilsley) on the 24th or the 28th of May, that these plants should be reopened in order to conserve the food which, in spite of what any official says, is going to waste, and which, according to the statement of the Prime Minister on his return from England, is urgently required to-day. This food is going to waste, and will go to waste in far greater quantities unless the Department of Labour accept their responsibilities to-day, and do, as the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) suggested, stop passing the buck from one department to the other. Let us assume our responsibilities, and do so to-day.
I am not going into the rights or wrongs of the strike, but I say definitely, Mr. Speaker, that the international woodworkers of America have come this far. The men have agreed and guaranteed to re-man the plants with union labour. They offered to do so on Friday night, and the plants could have been working all day Saturday, all day Sunday and all day to-day if the government had accepted its responsibility, as I see it, and put in a con-

(roller. We did it some time ago in the case of the American Can plant. We did it after a lot of food had been wasted. Apparently we are adopting the same attitude to-day in so far as fruit, fish, milk and other products in British Columbia are concerned. Apparently the department does not realize that if we start these plants to-day hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of food will still be wasted in British Columbia because, by operating the plants on twenty-four hour shifts from now on, we cannot catch up.
To-day I tried to ask what I thought was a fair question, namely, when would the plants be opened if they were not opened to-day, and why were they not opened before? Every hon. member knows my stand in this matter; but I say that no union, no operator and no government can justify food going to waste by the buck being passed from the minister to the minister of labour of British Columbia or to the federal authorities at Ottawa or to the union. The unions are prepared to go to work to-night and work all night producing crates, barrels and other containers if the Minister of Labour of the federal government will put Mr. Jones or someone else in as controller to operate these plants for a period of at least three weeks during which time negotiations can be carried on.
A short time ago the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) showed me the latest edition of the Kamloops paper. These people know the situation in British Columbia; they know the situation in Kamloops, and! they state that if we operate to-day we shall still lose foodstuffs because we simply cannot catch up. Surely we are big enough or should be big enough to discuss these matters without prejudice to either side while the plants are operating. It could be done along the line of the appeal w7'hich was made by the Acting Prime Minister, and which has been answered by the International Woodworkers of British Columbia, If the appeal of the Acting Prime Minister of May 27 has not been answered by the companies or the government, it has been answered by the union. Why not by the government and operators? I am now appealing to the Department of Labour of the federal government. I am appealing particularly to the. minister of that department. I shall not use the word I intended to use-
Use it.

No. The Minister of Labour is always good-natured; I shall say that for him. As a member of parliament representing the fruit-growers, I do not want any buck-passing or side-tracking. What I want the minister to do is to tell me when

these factories are to be reopened. If he cannot tell me that I should like to know why.
I should like to know why he cannot take some action when the men are prepared to go to work in the factories under a controller to prevent the fruit in British Columbia from wasting.

Signs of labour unrest are obvious all over the country, and part of the reason is that the government has not yet had the courage to face up to the inevitable results of its own policies. The Progressive Conservatives would like to see the ceilings lifted just as quickly as possible. The government intends to go about the matter more slowly, but no matter how slowly they go about it, nevertheless the fact remains that to the average worker his cost of living is increasing. The increase in the cost of living does not always mean a monetary increase. It may mean a depreciation in the quality of the goods he has bought.
One of the problems which is facing the average worker throughout this country is the increase in the cost of food, particularly milk. Milk is basic to the health of a nation; yet the price has gone up by two cents a quart, and within a few months there is the threat that it will go up still another two cents a quart. The ordinary working-class family know that the cost of clothes they have to buy is going up. They find the costs creeping up all around them, and if they are to live on a standard which will grant them the minimum amount of health, naturally they must have higher wages. The labour disputes to-day centre largely around the question of higher wages.
There is also the question of security in employment. We have heard almost ad nauseam of the government's promises during the election of jobs for all. We have read the government's white paper on employment policy, and seen how its policy was to provide full employment, whatever that may mean. But full employment is not with us, and there is no sign at all of full employment because there is no sign at all of a reconversion programme on the part of the government. There is no general all-out Canadian plan which will give the people an inkling as to wRat the government has in mind to maintain full employment. I should like to bring this matter particularly to the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) because full employment is largely a matter of fiscal policy, and we are faced with this apparent fact: according to the govern-63260-1621
ment's advisory committee on reconstruction, that is, the James committee, it is estimated that under full employment the savings of the Canadian people will be in the neighbourhood of $1,500 million a year. If we .are to maintain full employment the costs of industry have to come back again in the purchasing stream. I differ from my hon. friends of the Social Credit party in not believing there is an inherent deficiency of purchasing power under the present economic system. I believe every element of cost has an offsetting element in somebody's income. But when we have $1,500 million worth of savings, much of which is not reinvested in the economy, then there will be an apparent lack of purchasing power. When that lack of purchasing power appears profits diminish; because profits diminish there is a tendency to lay-off men or to cut wages, and when that is done purchasing power is still further diminished. It is true that one might perhaps stabilize the national income at $8 billion as one might stabilize it at $3 billion, as happened in the thirties, but on these low levels the obvious result is mass unemployment.
If we are to maintain full employment, obviously somehow or another the government must evolve a scheme whereby the savings of the people as a whole, the savings of industrial enterprise, will again be channeled back into purchasing power. Yet according to the Financial Post's 1944 survey of firms which, I think, accounted for, about sixty per cent of manufacturing industry, these companies figure on spending slightly more than than $100 million a year on capital assets. Mr. J. R. Beattie, of the Bank of Canada, writing in the August, 1944, issue of the Canadian Journal o) Economics and Political Science, pointed out:
(a)	That "even the tremendously rapid industrial expansion . . . during the war" had not "involved more than $1,000,000,000 of capital expenditure . . . public and private ... on plant, equipment and housing in any one year;"
(b)	that though "electric power is a heavy capital-using industry," its "pre-war investment in fixed assets was less than $1,500,000,000;"
(c)	that "one year's saving" at the rate of $1,500,000,000 a year "would more than cover the cost of all residential housing built in the twenty years from 1917 to 1937;" (d) that $1,500,000,000 "would cover nearly half the total fixed capital investment in Canadian railways;" (e) that "even the building of a new industry comparable to the pre-war automobile industry would absorb less than three weeks' saving at the rate of $1,500,000,000 a year."
That means there must be a tremendous amount of additional purchasing power spent if we are to maintain a balance between national income and the outgoings of the incomes whether they be wages or profits on
