*other income of the people. But now comes a new survey of post-war investment plans, in the Canadian Bank of Commerce monthly letter of January, 1946, which estimates that capital expenditure for the years 1946 to 1950 will be as follows:
City and town homes	 $750,000,000
Business building	 250,000,000
Industrial and mining	 1,000.000,000
Public utilities	 350,000,000
Transportation	 400,000,000
Farm improvement and extension	 350,000,000
That means a total in these years of $3,100 million, or a total per annum of $620,000,000; yet on the committee's estimate the Canadian people are going to save a billion and a half dollars each year. If we are to maintain full employment this means that somehow or another another $900,000,000 must be spent in this country, preferably in capital construction, or if not, then in improving the conditions of the people; and one way in which that is being done is through the children's allowances. The Minister of Finance cannot exempt himself from some responsibility for complete employment in this country. That is a problem he must face, and it is a problem for which we in the C.C.F. think we have an answer. It means the complete control of investment in this country by the government and investment channeled out so that, as a result, socially useful purposes shall be served. If in the forthcoming budget the Minister of Finance can give us no hope at all that this policy will be followed, then I think we can say with some certainty we are coming into a period of still further aggravated labour troubles and increased unemployment.
What I should like to speak of particularly at this moment is a matter affecting the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), because here I think he has been somewhat remiss in his responsibilities. I should like to remind the house again of a situation which exists in the city of Winnipeg and which is felt in other areas where these men have gone to live. In 1919 there was a general strike in Winnipeg, during which some four thousand workers of the Canadian Pacific Railway company went out on strike. Many were accepted back by the company, but the price they had to pay for reemployment was the giving up of all seniority rights before the strike. In tribute to the government-owned line, Canadian National Railways, let me say that they took back their men; and, when they established their pension fund in 1935 they gave all men, whether strikers or not, credit for every year and every month they had worked for the company. That was not the case with the Canadian Pacific. In 1937 this company instituted a

new pension plan on a contributory basis. Previously the pension plan had been on a noncontributory basis; and, when the men asked for higher wages the officials of the C.P.R. pointed to the pension plan and to their generosity in giving their men these pensions, and asked that this be taken into consideration. When the new plan was put into operation in 1937 it applied only to those of the age of forty and under. As a result, some four hundred elderly employees of the C.P.R. were given no pension rights at all. Some 2,100 others were affected because the time they had worked prior to the strike did not count toward their seniority. Mr. Coleman, who is now president of the Canadian Pacific Railway company, had a meeting with a sub-committee of the general chairmen of the union, and according to the union Mr. Coleman stated that it would take an additional $1,250,000 to meet the pensions which were asked. The report of the union goes on:
He made it very clear that the earnings of the company made such a task quite impossible, and regretted very much that, in such circumstances, he had to deny the request of the committee.
The subcommittee went on to say:
We are still of the unanimous view that, had the financial conditions of the company been different, we would have made progress.
The financial conditions of the company are appreciably different to-day, and I only hope the C.P.R. will take that fact into consideration when considering the claims of the men. The net income of the company in 1941 was some $46,000,000; in 1942 it was $48,000,000; in 1943 it amounted to $49,000,000, and last year it was some $31,000,000. It should be noted also that last year the profit and loss balance in the balance sheet amounted to $262,700,000. Out of that sum I should think the company could well afford to pay pensions to the men who are now leaving the employ of the company because of age and who are being wretchedly discriminated against because of the strike. The C.P.R. is one of the few companies, if not the only one, still treating in such a way the men who went on strike in Winnipeg in 1919. I have asked several questions of the Minister of Labour in that connection. Last December I asked what had happened to the report of the commissioner who had been appointed by the government to investigate the situation. The minister then told me that the report had been received and had been submitted to the company. Be it noted, Mr. Speaker, that this investigation was conducted at the request of the employees, not at the request of the company; yet the company was given the

Supply-Labour Conditions
privilege of seeing this report while it has been denied to the union. Again in May I asked the minister what the outcome of the investigation was. All he could tell me was that the Canadian Pacific Railway company were still considering the matter. Therefore I wrote Mr. Coleman to ask when we might expect the company to give the government its answer. I received a reply from Mr. Manson, vice-president in charge of personnel, who said in part:
The report of the investigator is being studied; and inasmuch as he required more than seven months to complete his findings, I am sure you will appreciate the time it takes to analyse the document.
That is a lot of unadulterated nonsense. It may take a commission seven months to make certain findings, but surely it does not take seven months to consider the advisability or otherwise of implementing those findings. However, that is the case put up by the Canadian Pacific Railway company, so that I hope the Minister of Labour will get some iron into his spine and go after the C.P.R. to learn exactly what they intend to do about the legitimate plea of these men I have mentioned.
I do not take advice of that kind from a jellyfish in Winnipeg.

I think the minister should take the advice, because he is badly in need of it.
There is another thing. There is a dispute to-day between the typographical unions and newspapers in Vancouver, Edmonton, Hamilton, Ottawa and Winnipeg. I asked the minister, at page 2153 of Hansard, the following question in reference to this dispute:
I wish to direct to the Minister of Labour a question of which I have given him notice. What steps are being taken by the federal government to settle the dispute between the typographical union and the newspapers concerned?
Part of his answer was as follows:
In Winnipeg, basically the issues were the union's policy that its international law is not subject to arbitration, et cetera-and when I say "et cetera" I refer to the regulations set in motion by the respective governments of this country-the forty-hour week and payment for overtime if the union could not provide labour under its closed shop agreement. Unfortunately the situation had deteriorated to such an extent in Winnipeg by the time it reached the attention of my department that the appointment of two industrial disputes inquiry commissions and the holding of several conferences in Ottawa did not bring about a settlement.
I bring to the minister's attention the words, "unfortunately the situation had deteriorated to such an extent in Winnipeg by the time it reached the attention of my department". The minister may not like taking advice from the
hon. member from Winnipeg North; but let me say one thing more, and that is that his answers ought to be more accurate. This one is grossly and obviously inaccurate, on the basis of an answer to a question I asked later.
This is what appeared at page 2418 of Hansard:
Mr. Stewart (Winnipeg North):
1.	On what date did the dispute between the *typographical union and the newspaper publishers in Winnipeg start?
The answer to that was:
1.	The stoppage of work affecting the international typographical union and the Winnipeg Tribune and Free Press commenced on November 8, 1945, being the culmination of a dispute which had been developing for some weeks previously because of failure to agree on the terms of a new agreement to replace one which had expired September 30, 1945.
The second question was:
2.	On what date was the department made cognizant of the dispute?
And the answer:
2.	On October 31 my department received information that a dispute existed and that a strike was possible. On November 1,-
That was seven days before the lock-out took place.
-the publishers of the two newspapers requested the intervention of either a conciliation officer or an industrial disputes inquiry commission. A conciliation officer was appointed on November 2.
The dispute started on November 8. The third question was:
3.	On what date was Mr. Justice Major appointed as a commissioner to investigate the dispute ?
And the answer:
3.	Mr. Justice Major was appointed a commissioner on November 9.
The Minister of Labour says that the situation had deteriorated before it reached the attention of his department. Yet, nine days before the lockout took place, the Minister of Labour had acted-and I think rightly so; I do not blame him for it; rather, I give him credit. The day after the dispute actually took place, a conciliation officer was appointed. As I said, the first answer given by the Minister of Labour was not altogether accurate.
Last summer the Canadian newspaper publishers association held a meeting in eastern Canada. I do not pretend to know what went on there, but I do know that not long after that, when the union agreement in AVinnipeg was up for negotiation, certain publishers balked, insisting that the laws of the union had to be arbitrated. That had never been the case before in the history of that union. Never at any time in all its eighty years have the union refused to arbitrate hours,
Supply-Labour Conditions

wages or conditions of an agreement. But they have always insisted that the laws of their own union were not arbitrable, and properly so; because were the laws of the union arbitrable, in every city one would find a hundred different interpretations of the law.
Would the hon. member take the stand that the rules of the trade union take precedence over the laws of this country.

No, I did not say that the laws of the trade union should take precedence over the laws of this country, because the trade union have stated that the law of Canada takes precedence over the law of their union. So that that is no argument.
You are talking about something you know nothing about.

I am talking about something concerning which I know a lot more than you do, because I have been with the men, talked the matter over with them, and they know what they are talking about, even though the Minister of Labour may not know. There can be only one interpretation of the law of the union, and that is the interpretation they put on the law themselves, because those laws are there for the government of the union, and for nothing else.
It has been said-I have seen it in print-[DOT] that the printers are trying to compel publishers to publish what the printers want. That is obviously nonsense. The position taken by the typographical union throughout the years proves that that is nonsense; and it is nonsensical to say that this is a case of foreign interference in Canadian affairs. Each individual union, on its own behalf, took strike action; and that action was not dictated by the international president, Mr. Randolph or by anybody else.
There is much less foreign interference in the unions than there is foreign interference in business. When we consider that several billions of dollars of United States capital is invested in this country, I think we must begin to realize the amount of the United States interference there is in Canadian industry.
The Minister of Labour appointed Mr. Justice Major to act as commissioner, and the commissioner, I believe, did his best. He offered to the union six points to be decided upon, and stated that if the union agreed to them he would then persuade the publishers to agree to them, too. The union agreed to

four of them, and they said they were willing to discuss the remaining two, and to negotiate in that regard.
The publishers refused to have anything to do with the matter at all; they virtually walked out on the commissioner. The result is that to-day all across Canada we find these strikes in publishing plants; and unless some definite action is taken, and taken quickly, I fear they will spread. We find these strikes not only in the newspaper industry, but threatened in steel and among electrical workers. Practically every organized union in the country is affected.
Nobody likes to strike. Strikes cost the country money. They cost the workers money. They cost the employers money. But a worker goes on strike only as an act of desperation, only when that is the only way he can bring his case before the people. When a worker goes on strike he knows what the cost will be to himself and his family.
It is the responsibility of the federal government to take some active stand, a more definite stand than it has taken, in trying to act as conciliator between the conflicting groups in this country. It is the duty and responsibility of the federal government, where necessary, to take over plants which are concerned. They should be taken over on one basis; that is, that any profits accruing to those plants while they are being operated by the federal government should revert to the federal treasury.

Mr. Speaker, I should like for a moment to refer to what has been said by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) where he pointed out that the advocacy by the Social Credit party of a sufficiency of purchasing power would not solve the problem. I remind the hon. member that labour unions are now on strike to obtain increased purchasing power. The Social Credit party contends that if labour unions were to receive their increase in wages, which we think they deserve, that would solve the whole problem. It must be remembered that the people at large would not get that increase; and therefore they would not be able to buy the goods which industry has produced.
However, I do not intend to enter upon an explanation of social credit theory for the special benefit of the hon. member for Winnipeg North, because I have come to the conclusion that he does not understand even the policy of socialism of the party to which he belongs. The hon. member said that his party stood for complete control of investment. That was not the policy enunciated the other day by the hon. member for Vancouver East

Supply-Labour Conditions
(Mr. Maclnnis), when he stated quite clearly that he advocated the total ownership of the means of life.
I do not dispute one or the other, but I believe that the hon. member for Vancouver East came more closely to socialistic doctrine than did the hon. member for Winnipeg North, and I suggest that the latter named hon. member should study the policy of his own party before he begins to criticize others.
I should like to draw the attention of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) to conditions among labour in Canada. Only to-day I received two telegrams from labour unions, one at Drumheller and one at Calgary, asking me to do what I could to draw the attention of the government to the state of unrest among labour throughout Canada. Labour realizes that these continued strikes are not in the best interests of the country as a whole, and I believe they are just as anxious and ready as anyone else to have matters settled. But the government cannot take the attitude that it will sit idly by and let the strikes continue, in the hope that they will work themselves out in a natural way.
I do not think the minister did much to lessen unrest among labour when he stated the other day that he blamed strikes on communists, and said that if the communists wanted a fight he was ready to give it to them. I do not think the labour unrest in this country is due to communist elements. Men are striking for legitimate reasons. The minister knows as well as the rest of us that living costs are increasing rapidly. That being so, of necessity labour must be concerned about its standard of living. As prices go up, the standard of living comes down. Not only must labour be concerned about that; the rest of the people of Canada are much concerned because these continued strikes are bound to add to the increased cost of goods.
I think the question was brought up timely by the hon. member when he spoke this afternoon. I do not intend to enter into a lengthy discussion on labour, but I suggest to the government that they will have to do something definite to solve these problems or labour and the employers will have to deal with the matter to see if settlements cannot be brought about. It would be much better if the government had some definite plan in mind so that when a strike occurs they could insist upon a settlement.
Does my hon. friend suggest compulsory arbitration?

I do not think it needs compulsion on the part of the government or on the part of labour or on the part of the
employers. There should be some reconciliation between the three groups. If no settlement can be arrived at between labour and the employer, then the government should step in and do something. They should not stand idly by while conditions get worse and worse. It is no solution of the problem for the government to say that we have less labour trouble in Canada than in any other country in the world. If conditions do not improve quickly we shall soon reach a point where Canada will be leading the world with labour troubles.
We had better get busy. The government should have some definite policy. They should enact some regulations which would bring these strikes to an end so that the country can get on with the production that is so greatly needed.
Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Veterans Affairs): I should1 like to take only one or two minutes to deal the the remarks made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken), who has raised objection to calling three new departments in committee of supply, not for the purpose of discussion but simply to get them in. The situation is that at the present moment we 'have eleven departments in supply. One department, the Department of Agriculture, is almost completed, as is the Department of National Health and Welfare. There are eleven departments not yet in supply. The theory that getting a department into supply at an early stage deprives hon. members of the right of expression and the opportunity to ask for the redress of grievances is an entire fallacy. If a department already in supply is called' on Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday every hon. member has the right to debate the motion.
If -the record of this session is read it will be found that supply was called earlier and has been called more frequently than in any session during the fifteen years I have been in this house. H-on. members opposite must accept some responsibility for moving a motion of no confidence and holding up supply for two weeks. Hon. gentlemen must realize that every session complaints are made in the last week or -two weeks about the government, no matter who the government is, because of th-e congestion of the estimates. We have tried to avoid that this session. We are trying to get departments into supply, but when we do so we are met with retarding suggestions by hon. gentlemen opposite. I will meet the suggestion of the leader of the opposition and call two departments to-day and two next Monday, and I ho-pe the house will agree to that.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to follow up the remarks of the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank). A few days ago the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Ilsley) made an appeal for the operation of these plants in order that containers might be provided for food. I know that right after that the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) became very active. No hon. member from British Columbia has done more in connection with the settlement of this strike than the hon. member for Fraser Valley. He has spent in the neighbourhood of $200 on telephone messages; he has met with union representatives, and he has spent a considerable amount on telegrams. Along with other hon. members, I have personal knowledge of the work he has been doing.
Following the appeal of the Acting Prime Minister, and largely because of what was done by one private member of this house with the support of other hon. members, the union have agreed to go back to work in these factories if the government will put a controller in charge and agree that negotiations shall continue while they are at work. We cannot understand why the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) will not take that action at this time when British Columbia is short of containers for fruit and other perishable products.
Even if these factories commence operations at the present time the tree fruit industry-the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) will agree with this statement.-will be short of containers this year. What is the reason for the delay in this action? Most people know that in British Columbia within three or four weeks it is customary, particularly in the coast area, for the logging companies to shut down on account of the hazardous fire situation. Cannot the Minister of Labour visualize; cannot he possibly see that, if this dispute is prolonged any longer and the fire season comes, we shall then have a heavy slugging match between the big operators in British Columbia and the union? That would be a most deplorable situation. It would not benefit the strikers or the operators or the community. I urge the minister to give consideration to the appointment of a controller in the box manufacturing and container manufacturing plants. That at least w'ould be a step in the right direction.

The hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) this afternoon referred to some facts which I brought to his attention appearing in the Kamloops Sentinel, which I received to-day. For the information of the house and the

Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) I should like to give these facts and figures to reinforce what has already been said with regard to the strike. In its issue of June 12 the Kamloops Sentinel reports an address by a veteran mill-man before the board of trade, in which the speaker said:
The box requirements of the whole upcoun-try's fruit and vegetable industry represent 55,000,000 feet of timber. It would be physically impossible for the mills to saw this amount in the time left before the harvest is in full flood.
The 460,000 fruit and vegetable containers needed for the Kamloops district's crop represent 20,000.000 feet of lumber. Only 50,000 of the boxes have been processed.
Further down:
The grower's survey led to the conclusion that "even if the mills resumed production to-morrow there probably would not be enough shooks produced to market the province's crops."
Dealing with the Okanagan valley, it has this to say:
At Penticton it was estimated that if production had resumed June 10 there should be enough containers to handle the big crop. After that date there would be a daily shortage of
5.000	boxes-a potential money value loss of $10,000 daily.
At Summerland the picture was even glimmer. The mill advised growers some time ago it could not supply the shooks ordered even if plant operation were not interrupted. Every day this mill is strike-bound 8,000 apple boxes are lost and the growers lose about $16,000 daily. No cherry boxes have yet been delivered.
At Kelowna, Simpson's, the largest mill in the interior, despite fairly steady operations from October to May 17, had delivered only slightly over 40 per cent of shooks ordered. At normal production rate it will require five months to catch up with orders. Capacity of the plant is determined by lumber supplied and it is short nearly 3,000,000 feet. It can produce 10,000 apple boxes a day.
At Vernon growers estimate a shortage of
8.000	boxes daily, with ia daily loss to the community of $16,000.
There is a good deal more of the same sort of facts, but I think I have given sufficient in concrete proof of the loss facing the people in the interior of British Columbia.
As regards the strike itself, there have been some developments which have not perhaps been brought out in the statements made here in the house. One of the most interesting ones is that the union made a proposal to the British Columbia fruit growers' association that if they would support the union's wage and certain other demands they would put men back into the box factories. There was great hope that that would produce a resumption of work in the box factories, but it did not take place for the following reason- I am quoting from the same article:
The union, according to J. R. J. Stirling, the president of the association, also reserved the right to stipulate which employees could work during the truce because "there were certain former mill employees whom the union would not recognize."
The growers' association countered with an offer whereby the box factory employees would return under pre-strike conditions, with tne British Columbia fruit growers' association guaranteeing to the workers the award on which the strike is eventually composed.
Also blocking acceptance of the I.W.A.'s three-week "truce" proposal was the reaction of national war labour board, when questioned by the British Columbia fruit growers' association as to the legal position.
I should like the Minister of Labour to listen to this because I am going to ask him some questions arising out of it.
Ask all the questions you want.

The minister is in an unusually generous mood. Perhaps he can produce a settlement of the strike. The article goes on:
The national war labour board declared that there could be no conciliation until the men returned to work on the pre-strike basis, and the board also announced it would not authorize any wage increase such as set out in the union's "truce" offer.
The regional w-ar labour board also indicated that there would be no isolated local increase in wages such as might come about if, for instance, a group of growers in desperate need of boxes underwrote the operation of a box factory on the I.W.A. basis.
So that hope of resumption of work in the box factories came to nothing.
In the previous discussion on this question, several hon. members suggested' that in order to provide a means of settling and preventing strikes a labour code should be devised. This question has received considerable discussion. The only existing labour code is P.C. 1003. It perhaps would not be well to go into the merits or demerits of P.C. 1003, but such as it is, it is the only labour code we have. It is my understanding that it does provide a set of rules by which disputes may be submitted to arbitration and in accordance with which they should be settled. That constitutes a set of rules which must be complied with before a strike can be called. If my understanding is not correct, I would appreciate it if the Minister of Labour would correct it. The merits or demerits of the code do not enter into the question. It is the only code we have. I would ask the Minister of Labour this question. Is the present lumber strike in British Columbia an illegal strike in view of the terms of P.C. 1003? If so, why have not the penalty terms of that order been complied with in an effort to end the strike?

L would appreciate it if the minister would answer these questions. In conjunction with other members from British Columbia, I would urge him to lose no time in appointing a controller in the box factories in an effort to get the men back to work.

I have listened to the hon. members here this afternoon and I was particularly impressed by the speech made by my hon. friend the member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis). I do not think anything is to be gained by trying to be clever or smart, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) tried to be this afternoon. When he gets older and has more experience in this chamber he will understand that we can carry on only by being decent to one another, instead of sinking into the gutter like he did this afternoon.
No one underestimates the difficulties and complexities of the present situation. While the final responsibility rests upon myself, I think there is a responsibility on every member of this House of Commons, when he rises in his place, to give at least some leadership. Here we are passing through a difficult period in which we find an emotional breakdown after a long war. I do not believe that there is any short-cut to the settlement of industrial disputes. I have had enough experience to understand that. I also know that all the faults are not on one side. I know, of course, that politically it is always best to take the side of the larger numbers. You are not taking any chances when you do that; it is a perfectly safe thing to do. But what we are endeavouring to do in this country-I speak of the Canadian people generally-and what this House of Commons irrespective of party is trying to do, is, I believe, to protect the living standards of the great masses of the people of this dominion. I say that without any equivocation. While our approach may be different, I think that in the main that is the underlying motive of all the members of this chamber.
There is a philosophy or an ideology of government which holds that when you debase the currency, revolution is around the corner. There is no secret about that. Lenin preached it prior to the 1917 revolution in Russia. You may have read in last week's Newsweek what Mr. Earl Browder recently said in Moscow. In effect, what he said was that, now that the war is over, the more strikes we have, the nearer the revolution is. That is a matter of record. I say sincerely that I believe more can be done by negotiation and conciliation than in any other way. One of the Social

Credit members spoke this afternoon about compulsory arbitration. I do not think he understood the import of his language.
I did not say "compulsory" arbitration.
Wait a minute. I listened to you. Now let me speak.
Then get it right.
The effect of what the hon. member said was compulsory arbitration.
No such thing.
If you say a thing you have to take the other fellow's interpretation. This is still a free country. I say that the import of my hon. friend's remarks was that there should be compulsory arbitration.
It was no such a thing. That is the minister's misinterpretation of it.

I shall be charitable to my hon. friend. Probably he meant nothing at all. However, if I cannot satisfy him, for goodness' sake let me say something of what I feel about compulsory arbitration. Neither employers' organizations nor labour organizations in North America agree with the principle of compulsory arbitration. Conditions are always difficult when one side says, "Now this is as far as we are going; we won't go any farther." The greatest progress has been made by labour and employers' organizations in this country when there has been a willingness to give and take, without resort to what labour men call the economic arm of the labour movement. As I said before, we have been reasonably successful. When you reflect that under the wartime labour relations order there have been thirty-two hundred odd cases, and only eight strikes, I think that is a pretty fair batting average.
The hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) talked about an offer which he had received from some individual in connection with this dispute in British Columbia, to put these plants back into operation. He may have received it, but I did not. He showed me the wire, and I had the information relayed back to British Columbia, but we did not get the same kind of answer which he got from this individual. I believe that the offer of fifteen cents an hour and the revocable check-off is a fair compromise and that there is no sufficient reason for the non-acceptance of that offer by the trade union out there. At the same time I would say to the shipping companies on the great lakes that the 84-hour week is a relic of bygone days of industrial operations. Let us be frank about the mat-

Supply-Labour Conditions
ter; in this day and age, any group of employers who think they can put over the proposition of a 12-hour day and a 7-day week might as well try to push back the St. Lawrence. It cannot be done. I believe that, given the right degree of conciliation in both these disputes, there is absolutely no reason why they should have ever started. Working people never win by a strike. The leaders may get prominence; they may make a national reputation for themselves; but the men and women back in the trenches, the rank and file, have to sacrifice so heavily that often it takes them a long time to recover, and sometimes they never catch up. I believe that succecs in industrial leadership, whether on the part of employers or employees, requires them to have some regard for the rank and file. They are simple people, like myself, they have a spark of the divine in their make-up, and I believe that sometimes these "ships that pass in the night" are not giving the leadership which the workers justly desire and deserve.
Coming to the question of "passing the buck," let me tell the hon. member from British Columbia who raised it that I am not given to that practice, and the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine) knows it very well. I accept full responsibility in the matter of the British Columbia dispute so far as my responsibility goes. But by the very nature of things, having been asked by the minister of labour of British Columbia to appoint a commissioner, I must confer with him and the commissioner in connection with the settlement of this dispute. Obviously the federal Minister of Labour in a country as vast as Canada cannot be responsible for every dispute which takes place anywhere in any province. I believe every hon. member will recognize that. In the course of time, and in my opinion within not a very long time, the constitutional jurisdiction in connection with labour disputes will have to be returned to the provinces. There is a good deal of sloppy talk about the centralization of power; but, as any lawyer knows, you cannot break a law by agreement. The only reason we have a national labour code in this country at the moment is that the power was included in the jurisdiction of my department under the War Measures Act. My hon. friends opposite have their opinions about legislation by order in council, and I hope it will be possible in the not very distant future to put the jurisdiction back where it properly belongs.
It is getting near six o'clock, and I have said all that I care to say at the moment. Hon. members can rest assured that when responsibility in relation to the settlement of these disputes is placed upon me, I will not shirk it.

Did the minister intend to answer the question about P.C. 1003?
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) neglected to answer two questions I asked him just before the house rose at six o'clock. I wonder whether the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine) would be kind enough to permit the minister to give the answers now. I asked whether the lumbermen's strike in British Columbia is an illegal strike within the meaning of order in council P.C. 1003? If so, why are the provisions of that order in council not applied?
I cannot answer without the unanimous consent of the house.
I appreciate that.

The discussion on the motion to go into supply has ranged over a rather wide field. Under such circumstances it is the privilege, of course, of an hon. member to bring forward whatever matter seems to him to have some importance; but the discussion as opened by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Mac-Innis) had to do with the two main strikes now in process in Canada, and I intend to say what I wish to say on this matter and, if possible, to bring the attention of the house back to that issue in particular.
I listened, as I always do, with great interest to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) in his reply. I was particularly struck with the remark which he made as regards the responsibility of members of the house as well as the responsibility which devolves upon him as Minister of Labour. With that I wholeheartedly agree; and it is because I have some feeling of responsibility as a representative in this house, and feel something of the urgency of the subject itself, that I make the remarks that I am about to make.
I should like to say also that I appreciate perhaps more than most the abilities of the minister. I appreciate some of the problems with which he has to contend, and I hope that nothing that I say will ruffle his feelings or make his problem any more difficult; for it is most certainly something that I do not wish to do. But having said that, I would say
Supply-Labour Conditions

that his speech was more discouraging than I felt it ought to be in the circumstances. Ho gave us a few homely truths which I do not suppose anybody will dispute; in fact they are so commonplace and so well known as to be almost hackneyed. He told us. very truly, that there are no short-cuts to settling strikes of this kind. He also said that there are faults on both sides-there usually are. We all agree that these two things are true in this strike as in many others. But it must be a challenge to the genius of the minister himself and to the imagination of this house to find as short a cut as possible to settle the strike, to find out on which side the greatest fault lies, and to find a method of bringing some measure of justice to bear upon the situation.
I believe the minister allows a prejudice which many people feel against communism to influence his mind in this matter. He referred to some speech that a Mr. Browder had made in Russia to the effect that the more strikes we had the better for the revolution, or something to that effect. I am not very much interested in Mr. Browder or in his views in so far as they apply to the present situation. It may very well be that there are communists in the leadership of this strike; I do not know; but I do not think that it is the point at issue with us here. It is far more important that we should examine the conditions of the workers who are taking part in these strikes and satisfy ourselves that there is or is not, as the case may be, a just cause for these strikes. If there is a just cause for the strikes, then we must not allow our prejudice against any particular leader to prevent us from seeing that justice is done.
The minister himself roundly condemned the 84-hour w'eek and said in language something like this, that you might as well try to push back the St. Lawrence as to prevent the ultimate coming of the 8-hour day. He says that it cannot be done. But the great fact is that it is being done; that it is going on before the minister's face and before our faces while we are talking about it. Therefore there is no use saying that it cannot be done. It is being done and we are faced with that outstanding fact.
I should like to point out that, according to the information which I have, there are some 5,800 seamen affected by the seamen's strike. I am informed that there are as many as 37,000 affected by the woodworkers' strike in British Columbia. To imply that we should be careless about taking active part in settling a strike because it is alleged that some communist is in the leadership-I may not be interpreting the minister's remarks

aright, but that is how I got it-is to ignore the actual conditions which govern the lives of 37,000 men in British Columbia and 5,800 seamen. That is the point that we must, centre our attention on.
The Canadian great lakes seamen work twelve hours a day seven days a week. That is the first fact. That is the pivot of the-strike. That is the condition for which they are seeking a remedy. The question which we have to ask ourselves is whether that is a. reasonable demand of men in this age; or if it is reasonable for shipowners to use all their power, all their skill and all their finances to. prevent such a thing from happening. It seems to me that should be the chief business of the representatives of the people in this house, because this is not merely a matter-of the wage-earners; it is not a matter merely of the shipowners, or both of them. It is a: matter of the economic life of this nation. It is also a matter of particular urgency because of world conditions as we know them. To-day we heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) review what he said appeared to be a dangerous situation in the world, and' say that he thought more production and! better distribution were the best remedy he-could see for the world problem. I think; most of us will agree, but here is a situation in which production has stopped and distribution has ceased; and by permitting that to go on we are increasing the dangers to which the. Prime Minister made reference this afternoon..
The 8-hour day for seamen was recommended by the international labour office of the league of nations in 1920. That was a long time ago, and this house has had ample opportunity to take some action on that question. I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) that since these seamen are not confined to one province ; since they are on the oceans on both sides of the country and sail the great lakes in the centre of Canada, it is not a matter which any provincial government can handle. It is specifically a matter for the federal government to take a hand in. I suggest that the seamen's strike for an 8-hour day should never have happened in Canada; that legislation should have been passed long since making it illegal for men to have to work twelve hours a day seven days a week or lose their jobs. I am not saying that all the responsibility or blame should fall upon the Minister of Labour. I accept my share of that responsibility, together with all other hon. members; but I insist that this is something which ought to have been done long ago. When I speak of that recommendation, though it was endorsed by

Supply-Labour Conditions
the delegates representing Canada it has never been ratified by this house, and most certainly it never has been implemented.
This condition, then, in my opinion should have been corrected by legislation; but instead of that being done, I am informed that when a certain company offered to introduce the 8-hour day on the great lakes the war labour board refused to countenance it. I am quoting now from the brief of the Canadian seamen's union, which says:
Recently the Imperial Oil and the McColl-Frontenac Oil Company, who operate oil tankers on the lakes, applied to the national war labour board for permission to abolish the 84-hour week and to replace it with the eight-hour day, 56-hour week. Unbelievable though it may sound, the war labour board so interpreted P.C. 9384 that they refused these oil companies the right to introduce the eight-hour day.
If I may point out to my hon. friend, that is not a statement of fact. The war labour board approved the 8-hour day on that application.
The minister says that is not a statement of fact. Then, of course, the judgment must lie as between the minister and the brief, and I am not competent to judge as between the two.
I am saying that on my responsibility as a minister; that the war labour board approved the 8-hour day on the application to which my hon. friend has referred. That is Imperial Oil, is it?
Yes.
Then that was approved.

Well, as I say, Mr. Speaker,
I shall leave the minister and those who drew up the brief to settle that matter; but it is not too late yet for the government to act.
I am talking about the judgment of the board. I am not talking about something which was *written by somebody else, probably for propaganda purposes.

I have no intention of disputing the minister's word. I merely quoted what was given to me as fact. Personally I do not know which is the fact. I must take one or the other, or both, or neither; perhaps -in the long run I may take neither, but for the present I must accept the minister's statement. It is urgent, however, that our ships should be running now as they never ran before. The need for them is even greater, if that be possible, than during the war years. I suggest that the minister now introduce legislation for an 8-hour day for the seamen of Canada and that it be rushed through, with the three readings at one sitting if necessary, thus making it illegal for the shipowners to
have men working twelve hours a day on their ships; and failing that, to put in a controller and take over the shipping until such time as settlement has been reached. I need hardly point out that the 8-hour day for sailors is universally accepted. Certainly it is accepted in the United States, in Great Britain, in New Zealand, in Australia, and, indeed, in all other forward-looking countries. How is it that Canada should be so backward in a matter of this kind?
I think we should note also that the seamen's union did not press for the 8-hour day during the war period. They did not permit anything to interfere with the uninterrupted operation of Canada's merchant marine. It is worth noting also that a thousand of these men went down with Canadian ships while carrying on the business of war. I think we ought to be a little more considerate of their case when we realize the real sacrifices they have made and are making to the economic life of Canada. The 8-hour day was promised by the shipowners during the war. They said that when the war was over the 8-hour day would be granted, but when the war was ended the shipowners refused to keep their promise. In 1945, when the unions were negotiating the agreement under which they were operating before the strike took place, they pressed their claim again. Still the shipowners refused, and the agreement under which they were operating was signed only after a clause had been included which permitted the renegotiation of any clause to take place on the giving of ten days' notice by either of the parties.
So it is not true, as someone has suggested, to say that in calling this strike these men have violated their trust with the employers. However, the union took advantage of this clause to call the strike when they had failed to negotiate satisfactory arrangements with the shipowners. But even when the strike had been called, they still strove to have it settled by negotiation before the actual strike took place. Accordingly they applied to the Minister of Labour. The minister acted. I understand he called a conference for April 8. On that date representatives of the unions appeared, but the shipowners had disappeared. They refused to meet; hence the conference was abortive.
Having failed in this, the union called their strike on April 9, or at least called a strike vote; whereupon the ship owners countered with expensive and elaborate advertising in many of the daily papers of Canada, issuing strong press statements to the effect that they *would fight the seamen to the last against their demands for an 8-hour day.

We now come to the question: Can the shipowners afford to pay for an 8-hour day? I am not going to enter into the profits they made during the war, although that might very well be done. But I would say that morally this nation cannot afford to allow the continuation of a 12-hour day, seven days a week. Any industry which cannot afford to employ its men on an 8-hour day should either cease operation or be subsidized by the, public, so that one class of worker may not have to bear more than its share of the national burden.
United States lake shipowners have an 8-hour day. Not only do they have an 8-hour day; they pay from 50 per cent to 95 per cent higher wages each month to their men than is paid by Canadian companies, and they receive exactly the same rates or charges for the freight they move. An American able seaman on the lakes receives $216 a month for an 8-hour day, while a Canadian able seaman receives $112 a month for a 12-hour day.
And board, in both cases.
Yes.

Making
another $50.

That is for both, and does not alter the relationship. An American deckhand receives $166 for an 8-hour day, while the Canadian dteck-hand receives $89 for a 12-hour day, despite the fact that both companies charge the same rate.
Here is a Canadian ship loading grain in a Canadian port alongside a United States ship loading grain from the same elevator. They are both bound for the same port; both carry the same grain for the same freight rate. Yet there is this differential both in hours of labour and in, wages paid as between the United States and Canadian companies.
Those of us who are proud of Canada, and are going some day to be proud of the Canadian flag waving over us, ought to see to it that under that flag our working people have at least as good a chance to live as those under any other flag in the world. If the United States companies can afford1 to pay the wages they are paying, and give an 8-hour day to their seamen, when they are hauling the same goods as our men are hauling for the same freight rates, then I want to know what justification there is for our permitting Canadian seamen to work twelve hours a day, seven days a week for almost half the wages being paid by competitive companies in another country.
I need hardly refer to the condition in connection with the great strike in British Columbia. Most of us are aware of the need

for more and more lumber. All hon. members have been impressed by the pleadings of the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruick-shank), and his efforts to save the fruit crops in his constituency and province. I am told they have in sight only about 40 per cent of the amount of lumber required to take care of the fruit crops this year. In a time, like this, when foodstuffs have greater value than ever before in the history of Canada, there is a real urgency for immediate action on the part of the house and of the Minister of Labour.
I would plead that we lay aside whatever prejudices we may have in respect of any particuiar individual in connection with the leadership of these strikes, that we look at the great number of men affected, that we examine the facts and the conditions under which they are -working, and that we take action on those grounds, and on no other.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to say a word to those who spoke this afternoon regarding the situation in British Columbia. First, may I comment upon the question asked by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton). I do not pretend for a moment to answer the question the minister was asked, because he answered his questions ably, himself.
But when the hon. member asks a question regarding an illegal strike I think we might as well face the facts. The unions draw up agreements with the owners of factories. Certain clauses appear in those agreements, one of which is that a fine of $20 and a gaol sentence shall apply to all strikers who shall participate in an illegal strike. How could you take 37,000 men who are on strike and put them in gaol, even if you did declare their strike illegal? It does not seem to make sense. We may as well face that fact, instead of saying to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), "Why do you not enforce this clause respecting illegal strikes"? It simply cannot be done. In future agreements drawn up between workers and either provincial or federal governments, I suggest that we should be more careful and not include in the orders in council clauses which cannot be reasonably enforced.
When I last spoke in the 'hous'e it was pointed out to the minister just how serious the strike had become, so far as its effect on the fruit crop was concerned. But as the strike continues, it begins to affect other branches of produce as well. As recently as Saturday last the hon. member for Fraser Valley and myself, who are members of the Fraser valley milk producers' association, received telegrams from that association saying

that if they did not receive barrels and boxes at an early day the canned milk and powdered milk which they produce for shipment to Great Britain could not be made available. As time goes on, we find matters getting worse every day.
I would refer for a moment to the strike which took place last fall. At that time cans already manufactured were available in the factories in British Columbia, but the workers went on strike and refused to allow the farmers who were growing peas to get cans from the factories. The farmers had to stand by and see their produce wilt and spoil. After days and days of loss, the government finally did step in and take charge of the situation, and some of the crop was saved. I appeal to the minister this evening not to allow this thing to go on and on until there is no crop and then in the last' days step in and take charge of some of these factories. At that time it may be too late.
I realize the difficulties faced by the minister. We all know that the unions want to force the government to use the big stick on the owners. We may as well be frank about the matter. If the government do that in one instance, they will have to do it in every instance that occurs across the country. These matters have not been stated until now, but we may as well face the facts, and I think what I have just mentioned are the facts of the situation.
I urge the minister to do what he did in the canners' strike. If he puts in a controller I feel reasonably sure that it will not be long before a complete settlement takes place. I am assured of that by those who are handling the situation in British Columbia.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended making a speech to-night, but I want to support once again the appeal made this afternoon to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruick-shank). As we approached the weekend we had high hopes that when Monday morning came around we would hear that this strike in British Columbia had been satisfactorily settled. I listened to the questions put to the minister this afternoon by the hon. member for Fraser Valley and the minister's answers. His answer to the first question was no, that the strike was not over. The second question was if he were going to put a controller into these plants and open them immediately, and the answer was no. I think that came more or less as a shock to many of us.

I did not say "no" to the second question.
Mr. CRUICIvSHANK: Oh, yes, you did.
Just wait a minute.

We have waited for
three weeks.
If I remember correctly, what I said was, "no", to the first question; and to the second question with reference to a controller, that consideration was being given.

That is exactly the answer that the minister gave to me personally last week. I appealed to him and showed him certain telegrams that we were receiving from some of the fruit growers of British Columbia.
If I might say to my hon. friend-
No; the minister made his speech this afternoon.
This is a matter of privilege.
The matter of privilege is always your way.

You cannot deal with one another on that basis.

On a question of privilege, I want to say to the minister right here and now that I have not repeated any of the conversation he had with me. I am merely stating the answer he gave in this house this afternoon.
That is changing your tune.

Hear, hear.
-has tried his best.

The minister should read the record of what he said this afternoon. The hon. member for Fraser Valley has tried consistently not to take sides in this dispute, and I have tried to do the same thing. I realized that the minister was doing his best through the appointed officials in British Columbia to settle this dispute. But what is the use of appealing for more and more production in Canada? I have listened to appeals such as that made this afternoon by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), and then I see the hypocritical attitude taken by the government in refusing to do something when there is an appeal from all over the country for immediate action.
As the minister said this afternoon, we *ought to deal with this matter constructively. I think every word I have said in this house so far regarding this strike situation has been constructive. I have tried to follow the position in which the minister found himself. But what do we have here? Week after week the strike is going on and day after day there is in British Columbia considerable loss of fruit which we can ill spare. This is fruit that should have been saved. We are told that even if the mills began to operate to-night they could not begin to supply containers for the fruit that is still to come. I appeal to the minister to put himself in solid with the people of British Columbia by placing a controller in these mills.
Would my hon. friend go in and knock the dollar down to seventy-five cents in Vancouver, British Columbia, and allow the working classes to suffer?

My appeal is to put in a controller at once and get these box factories opened. Then you can allow the ordinary procedure to work in order to settle the strike, no matter how long it takes. Why should so many innocent people suffer because of the attitude of this government? My appeal is to put in a controller and then let them work it out themselves, as I believe they will.

Mr. Speaker, I want to add my voice to those who are asking the minister to step in and take the necessary action to bring this [DOT]strike to an end. I do not suppose there is really anything I can say that has not been said this afternoon, and I am not going to speak very long. This afternoon the minister asked the members of the house for leadership. In my view the members of the house have given Iiim an almost unanimous expression of 
opinion. The members of his own party, the Progressive Conservative party, the C.C.F. and I believe the Social Credit party, although I am not certain because I have not heard them in this debate, will be behind him in taking whatever steps he finds necessary in the public interest to bring this strike to an end at once.
That is exactly what we said.

I was not in the house when the hon. member spoke. That is a simple proposition. Surely the minister must know that if he has the whole house behind him he has the country behind him. He can give the leadership that he spoke of to-day without any fear of any consequences ensuing therefrom.
If you take over the industry and they do not go back to work, what then?

All I can say to the minister is that we have in British Columbia a situation where the chief industry of the province is tied up by a strike affecting thirty-seven thousand people. The production of berries and all other forms of food is being affected, as well as lumber supplies for UNRRA and Great Britain and those required in Canada for housing purposes. All these activities have been stopped by this strike. The strike, incidentally, has been declared illegal by the provincial minister of labour. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) was asked to give his opinion on that point but so far he has not given it. We have had ample conciliation procedure, and we have had a report from a highly respected judge who knows the lumber business intimately from his own experience. His report has been made after a very fair and long hearing given to all parties. We have the Minister of Labour here saying that the union should accept that report not only as being a fair report but as being in the interests of the men themselves, because all this time they are losing wages. We have the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) calling for production. Most important of all perhaps, we have all the newspapers in British Columbia, the organs of public opinion, of absolutely one mind, that neither the interests of the operators nor the interests of the men are any longer the matter of prime importance, but that the interests of the people of Canada, and particularly of British Columbia, together with the needs of the whole world at this time, should be the dominent and compelling factors in this situation.

I think what is going through the minds of the members of this house is, first, the absolute necessity of constructive action being taken at once so that something will be saved of these supplies-
I am looking for a way out. Would my hon. friend give me an indication of constructive action? Would he conscript labour, or what would he do? Let us bring this out into the open.

The men have
offered to go back to work.

When the minister interrupted me with his questions-and I will come to them later-I was dealing with what I think are the two most important considerations. First, there is the necessity for speed so that something will be saved. Second, this house believes, certainly I believe, that the conciliation procedure provided by P.C. 1003 has been exhausted. We have been given no idea of what further steps the minister proposes to take. We have held off during the past weeks because we realized that there were conciliation procedures which could be followed and nobody wanted to make the minister's task more difficult. But when he spoke this afternoon he did not carry us anywhere past the provisions of P.C. 1003 or indicate to us any other measures that could be taken in a deadlock of this kind.
In normal deadlocks, once the conciliation procedure has failed, under our present law the parties are left to work out their own difficulties among themselves. But all members of the house are at one in believing that such a course cannot be followed in this case, but that some new departure in the realm of labour relations must be taken.
The minister asked me to say what further steps he could take. Naturally I am not as qualified as he is to indicate those steps. But I should have thought he had in mind several steps that he could take, and it makes me apprehensive that he should have asked me for advice because it indicates that apart from the appointment of a controller he feels there is nothing he can do.
Certainly the appointment of a controller of these plants would be one way in which a solution might be found. The minister suggests that the men might not go back to work. That is a chance that the minister must take, and from what I know of public opinion in this country, particularly in British Columbia, I believe that if the minister puts in a controller the men will go back to work. But if he should find that his fears are realized and that on putting in a controller the men will not go back to work, there may be other
ways of dealing with the situation. In this particular strike-and I say this without reference to any other labour disputes-because the situation is so serious and the people of Canada, with the exception of the leaders of this union, are at one that it should be settled at once, I suggest to the minister that this is one case where, even if he were reluctant to do it as he well might be in every case, he might well invoke the penalty provisions of P.C. 1003, not, as the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) said, against the innocent men who form this union, but rather against the central body that called this illegal strike and thereby put the whole public of Canada and the needs of so many people in other parts of the world in such peril.

I know this debate is becoming irksome to the members on the other side of the house. However. I consider this matter of greater importance than the new flag. The hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine) a few moments ago waved the flag a bit and said that he hoped that some day under that flag the conditions which the people of Canada fought for in two wars would become established. Of course, if waving the flag would solve this problem the Conservative party would have solved it years ago. But it is going to take more than just waving a flag.
We have been discussing in this house for weeks and weeks matters that are merely incidental in comparison with the major economic problems that face this country, and I say that after due consideration. I think the problem upon which the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) focused the attention of the house this afternoon is one upon which we might well spend two or three days of debate with a view to settling it. You can condemn the employers and you can condemn the men of the union, but in the final analysis it is the members of this House of Commons to whom the people of Canada are looking for advice and guidance in matters of this kind. They cannot be settled outside.
I am not going to deal with the woodworkers' problem in British Columbia because that has already been dealt with by the members from that province.
But we have had no answer yet.
Well, you voted for the government. You cannot blame me.

We might get some help from you.

The hon. member for Fraser Valley has done such a capable job himself that m.v assistance is hardly necessary. The hon. member for Vancouver East this afternoon focused attention specifically on the Canadian seamen's union disturbance and it is with that I shall deal. I have sat here and listened to the other members who have spoken, each discussing and developing the question from his own angle, and I think it must be obvious even to the minister that what he is doing will not settle these two strikes.
I am going to deal for a few minutes with the minister's difficulties. I think the machinery writh which the minister has to work to-day in the federal department of labour invites difficulties of this kind. It is .slow, cumbersome, legalistic, academic; it does not understand the basic problems of the workers, with the result that we have the kind of friction which has developed in this case. I have only to mention the steelworkers' union in Sydney. For four and a half years they have been patient and long-suffering, down on their knees, praying the regional and national war labour boards for a nickel to wipe out the differential in their wage rates. They are still praying, waiting and hoping. Fortunately the people of Nova Scotia have great patience. The seamen and the woodworkers are a little more impetuous, and as a result the minister has these difficulties on his hands. But I think the delay of four and a half years which I have mentioned is a good example of what I mean, and the case is still "in the slings". The seamen, heaven knows, have been waiting since 1920 for someone to implement the 8-hour day for them. Internationally, everybody said they were entitled to it, and twenty years is a long time to wait. But what I was going to point out to the minister is that the time to stop strikes is before they start, and if some attention had been paid to this problem a couple of months ago, instead of the government sitting back and waiting for a divine providence to intervene, the trouble might not have developed into a strike.
The minister is faced, in settling the difficulty with the seamen, with the unfortunate fact that the antagonisms which have been allowed to creep in will not be permitted to be forgotten for the next twenty years. I am sorry the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) is not in his seat at the moment, because I am going to be a bit legal at this time. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), of course, is interested in this too, and I am glad he is in his seat. The hon. member for
Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), some considerable time ago, and the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) raised in this house the question of the status under the Canada Shipping Act of Canadian seamen who were ordered by their union off their boats because of difficulties with their employers in a collective agreement under the Canada Shipping Act. Leaving a ship without the permission of the captain could be construed as deserting the ship, and so would bring the men under the criminal code. The minister at that time stated that it was not the problem of the Department of Transport, that the strikers more properly came within the scope of the criminal code. That is now evident, because these men were arrested for deserting their ship. Somebody asked the question this afternoon if they thought the laws of the union took precedence over the laws of the country. I say no; there is not any conflict. I went through the mill on this question, so that I know something about it; I had lawyers and judges waving their hands at me for some considerable time over it. Any trades union is entitled to make laws to discipline, regulate and guide its own members within its own jurisdiction without contravening any of the laws of the country. That decision was handed down at a time when I happened to be present. I do not say that it is in Beauchesne. Under the formula worked out by the government and accepted by the union, all employees are entitled to return to the ships except those who may have committed acts which brought them under the criminal code. In my opinion, when that strike terminates, any seamen who were on strike, regardless of their position at the present time, should go back to their ships, because the men who came off these boats and are now being tried under the criminal code merely obeyed the instructions of their organization, as other members did who came off later. The individual is not at fault, it is the organization which accepts responsibility; and by sending most of the seamen back, with that group out, and in the toils of the law, you are starting the first blacklist and providing legal machinery for discrimination. In my opinion all these men should be permitted to go back to their boats.
I said a moment ago that antagonisms have crept into this strike. When it developed first it was orderly and quiet. There were no disturbances. But I drew to the attention of the Minister of Justice in this house that there was a private detective agency in Montreal, the Fidelity Detective Agency, evidence of whose activities has been supplied to us by men who were hired by it. Accord-

ing to affidavits which are in our possession, men were paid S10 a day, provided with transportation in trucks, and sent to the city of Cornwall with instructions that they were to wreck the poolrooms and restaurants and get out of the city as fast as they could, so that these acts of lawlessness might be attributed to members of the seamen's union. Away back in 1909, 1910 and up to 1925 they took these protectors of private property, put them on horseback, and, armed with all the authority of the state, they would ride you off the sidewalk. That may not be his prerogative; the enforcement of the law may be in the hands of the provincial governments; but the Minister of Justice presides over a body in this country known as the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. It is exclusively under his direction and jurisdiction. If called upon they are required-

They are provincial
police in five provinces.
I did not hear the minister.
They are the only police force in five provinces. Some provinces have provincial police; some provinces avail themselves of the R.C.M.P.
Yes, but they can be called in to assist in any section of Canada regardless of the provincial police.
At the request of the local attorney general.

At the request of the local attorney general? Well, we notice that Mr. Blackwell in Ontario is not allergic to police, because he manages to wave his wand and get as many as he wants at any time. The R.C.M.P. were used in Windsor and in Cornwall, and in each case they were requisitioned from this city. If the Minister of Justice has not any prerogative with respect to enforcing the laws, I think this House of Commons, in view of the fact that we make the appropriations which maintain that force, should have some understanding as to what they should be used for. I am not critical of the R.C.M.P. in their ordinary duties, but I do not think it was ever the intention of those who first mobilized the force that they should be used as strike-breakers across
Canada when the workers of this country are looking for something to which they are legitimately entitled.
The Minister of Justice should accept some responsibility at least in investigating this detective agency which hired1 people in Montreal and shipped1 them to Cornwall with instructions to turn the public against the seamen who are on strike looking for the establishment of the 8-hour day and small increases in wages. It is time that we found out whether that kind of thing is to be permitted. I am reasonably certain that if this upheaval had not taken place in Cornwall and if McMaster had not established a recruiting agency-and I have an affidavit here with regard1 to McMaster which I shall read for the minister's benefit; it was sent to Mr. M. J. Coldwell-
The hon. member does not need to tell me anything about McMaster; I know all about him.
He is allowed to run wild in Montreal; to act as the A1 Capone of the shipping companies in organizing gangsters for the purpose of injecting them into a legitimate labour dispute in order-
The hon. member is not going to put these words into my mouth.
I did not.
"The moving finger writes and having writ moves on." Let me put the matter straight. I was speaking of McMaster as a trade unionist.
The minister laughs.

I appreciate the minister's position. As minister he has to be dignified and he cannot call a thug a thug. He has to call him Gentleman Jim or something of that kind. But I am in the habit of using plain English in matters of this kind. What I am concerned about is the pattern which is being developed in the seamen's strike, and which is apt to spread to other industries if they get away with it.
The minister will remember the little steel formula and the strike-breaking in the United States some years ago. They were successful in exposing it after a lot of men went to gaol, suffered injunctions, broken heads and the rest of it. We do not wish to go through that kind of thing in this country. In my opinion it is that kind of action which is making it difficult for the minister. You have the employer standing behind barbed wire, completely alienated from his employees. You have the employee who has seen that mess at Cornwall.

It is that complex which makes the employee feel .that the employer is the kind of a fellow who will secure a gun to shoot him so long as he does not get behind the eight-ball himself. I hold in my hand a letter which was written to Mr. M. J. Coldwell, House of Commons, Ottawa. It is dated June 16, 1946, and was written by the solicitor who is handling the affairs of the seamen's union. It is as follows:
You will possibly remember reading in the Toronto and Montreal newspapers of Friday about certain statements made by H. X. McMaster, president of the national shipping federation, to the effect that the Canadian seamen's union was planning sabotage on our ships in July and other illegal activities. He is further reported as having stated he had eight men who were available to support his statements. We have procured an affidavit from one of these alleged eight men. It gives you the real story behind his statements.
That is the relevant part of the letter to ;he hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. This is one of the affidavits which was secured in the province of Quebec. It is as follows:
Province of Quebec,

I. the undersigned. John MacPherson Osborne, merchant seaman, residing temporarily at 1434-
This fellow would not tell a lie. I continue.
-St. Urbain street in Montreal, domiciled in the city of Toronto, do hereby solemnly declare:
I am making this declaration of my own free will and volition.
