He asked me to try to form a policy committee of eight men, preferably members of the Canadian seamen's union, who were dissenters of the union and who-would be willing to create confusion and dissension within the ranks of the Canadian seamen's union for the benefit of the ship owners.
He asked me to get these men to meet with certain ship owners whom he did not name at the C.S.L. wharf office on Ottawa street, on June 14, 1946, at eight p.m.
Captain McMaster likewise stated to me that either during the day or during the evening or night of June 14 a "job" would be done either at the Lachine canal or in the Soulanges canal and that it would be made to appear as though the Canadian seamen's union were responsible for this proposed illegal act.
The affidavit is signed by Osborne and his solicitor.
What is the name of the solicitor.

The seamen's union solicitor is Irving Himel. The name of the individual before whom the affidavit was taken is Bernard S. Mergler. They are not Scotch. I continue with the affidavit:
As a matter of fact, on Wednesday night, June 12, at about nine p.m. I was taken to a home in Westmount by Mr. McMaster, where I was introduced to Captain Reoch and to Mr. Campbell, who was supposed to be the host. There were about eight other men there to whom I was not introduced, and I was told by Mr. McMaster that they all represented the owners of various shipping companies. I was questioned by some of the persons there as to what connections I could establish with the Canadian seamen's union and these ship ow'ners told me to keep in communication with Mr. McMaster who would advise me as to what to do.
It was obvious that from my conversations and from my dealings with Mr. McMaster that he was closely connected with and in close cooperation with the ship ^owners and he was endeavouring to break the Canadian seamen's union for the benefit of the ship owners.
In consideration for my cooperation, Mr. McMaster offered me a job as personnel director of a proposed national seamen's benevolent association which would serve as an employment agency7 for the ship owners.
I 'phoned C. Sauras at the Canadian seamen's union office in order to give him this information of my own free will.
And I make this solemn declaration . . .
It goes on to give the regular form of declaration. There are several others here which were taken from some of the thugs who were sent in to Cornwall by the detective agency. They were taken after they landed in hospital, and they state who hired them, what they were hired for, and what the remuneration was to be.
It is all right to stand up in the house and to pull the Minister of Labour to pieces, to blame everything on him. We shall hare to

Supply-Labour Conditions
remember that behind the scenes there are, in my opinion, greater influences in this country than the Minister of Labour or the government. There is an invisible government in this country, and that invisible government is the government which wields economic power. They are in a position to tell the Minister of Labour, or any shipping company, or any steel company, or textile company or packing house or any of these major organizations that they have to play ball or there will be no production. I believe that is going on to-day. I believe that will continue until, not only the minister, but each and every member of this House of Commons accepts the responsibility delegated to him by the constituency which sent him here, namely, to stand up and call a spade a spade.
A thing is right or it is wrong; and in my opinion in a country that has provincial police, mounted police and police of all descriptions it is wrong to allow a detective agency or a private concern of any kind to promote civil strife. They are making it difficult for the minister; they are confusing the public; they are trying to smash legitimate organizations, and it is time we all came to grips with that kind of thing and exposed it. If the only function that agency has to perform is to use hired thugs as catspaws when decent citizens of this country are merely trying to maintain decent standards; if private concerns have the right to promote the sort of thing that was promoted in Cornwall, then I think it is time we folded up and gave up the pretence that we are here representing the people and making laws that are fair and equitable to everybody.
I would not have taken part in the debate to-day at all but for the fact that I too listened to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) this afternoon. Some members of this group had the privilege of going to Europe in the latter part of 1944. I could not describe what I saw there then, and I can imagine the situation there now in the way of misery and human suffering. This is no time for strikes or interruptions of- production on this North American continent. I believe that if the workers of this country are met fairly and squarely, with the cards laid on the table, they will not want to interrupt production. They realized in fighting this war that it was our war; they know we must follow through and attain the objectives for which we fought. One of the first requisites is the establishment of decent standards of living in the countries devastated by war. We should keep our shoulders to the wheel. Every machine in this country to-day should be producing foodstuffs, clothing and everything we can
ship to these countries, because it is not going to be possible to solve the problem on this continent alone. The other countries have to be brought up, and we shall not be able to do this by fighting among ourselves and thinking in terms of thirty years ago, as those who are opposing the seamen's union are doing to-day.
I thought this sort of thing belonged in the past, hiring thugs to shoot people who are in legitimate organizations. I believe we should put our foot down and abolish these agencies if they serve no other purposes. They must be able-bodied men, and we should put them to work producing something instead of carrying on activity of that kind in this country in this day and age. There is no use in the Prime Minister going over to Europe and discussing the food problems of that continent with Attlee, Morrison, Cripps and these other people; seeing the situation as it exists there; coming back and trying to impress it upon us in this house and then, when he looks across the country, seeing the chaos which exists in the machinery of production, all over small, trivial matters. I have never yet met with any body of men who would not be fair and reasonable if you sat down with them and put the cards on the table face up. The only time they get suspicious and afraid of you, and do not trust you, is when they see the sort of activities that have been carried on in connection with this seamen's strike.
I see the Minister of Justice is in his seat now. I am not going to repeat everything I have said previously, but I say that the minister presides over the R.C.M.P. I believe they are a decent body of men-

Would the hon. gentleman permit an interruption, just to suggest this? I listened to what the hon. gentleman said; and if the things described in that affidavit actually took place I agree with everything he said about them. I agree it is outrageous that things like those could happen, but I wanted to suggest to the hon. member that he read the affidavit again now that the Minister of Justice is here. I suggest that this house has a right to know whether these things have taken place. The hon. member is good enough to allow me this interruption, and I should like to ask if he knows any of these men himself, if he thinks they are responsible people. From what he said I gathered that he did not know them. To me the whole thing sounded like a kind of Oppenheim story. If it is true we should know it, and I suggest he should
Supply-Labour Conditions

put it right up to the authorities, so that this house and this country may know if these things are true.

I have already read the entire document. It is on record, and the minister can read it in Hansard. I am quite prepared to accept the statements contained in it, because we did meet with this Mr. Irving Himel, the legal representative of the Canadian seamen's union who is handling this problem. We met with him personally, together with a member of the union; we discussed with them these affidavits, and I believe they are all certified. I do not think any lawyer in this country would draw up a document of that kind and send it to members of the House of Commons, requesting us to make use of it, if it were not true.
The local chief of police also made the same statement.

I think it would be imposing upon the time of the house to read it all again. The Minister of Justice can read in Hansard what I have said about the R.C.M.P., which comes under his department. They can be requisitioned from one end of this country to the other to engage in activities which, in my opinion, are beneath their dignity; that is, when they are called to take part in the sort of situation in connection with which they were sent to Cornwall, where private detective agencies were promoting civil strife and trying to blame it on the seamen's union. The R.C.M.P. should not be involved in a situation of that kind. I have too much respect for them to see them dragged into a mess like that. I do not think they were ever organized for that purpose. When I asked the minister a question in reference to this matter a few days ago he said it was not the prerogative of his department to enforce the laws. I quite agree, but I say that when a body such as the R.C.M.P., which functions under his department, is requisitioned for service in some part of the country, he should be reasonably sure that the service they are going to perform is in keeping with the purposes for which they were organized.
I suggest to the hon. gentleman that the R.C.M.P. had absolutely nothing to do with the mess he speaks of in Cornwall. They went there for one purpose only, to protect government property.
That is always the excuse. I have heard the same excuse for the last twenty-five years.
That is not an excuse; it is a fact.

Why were they not sent
there when these two truckloads of thugs from Montreal invaded Cornwall? One of the first people assaulted in the city of Cornwall was a sergeant of police, who was rescued by members of the Canadian seamen's union. There were no R.C.M.P. requisitioned then.
No. The hon. gentleman refers to an officer of the township police-[DOT]
Certainly.

-who was placed in that position. I may add that the chief of the township police investigated the circumstances to which my hon. friend refers and charged McMaster and several others, who are now before the Cornwall police court.
I know that; but you say-the mounted police were sent only there to-protect government property.
I say they had nothing to do with the mess to which my hon. friend refers.

They were sent to Windsor, also. They were not sent there to protect government property. That is always the excuse, you see, that it is government property or that it is private property; but the same consideration is not shown to those who established that property, who provided the labour and who should have an equity in the property, when they are trying to feed their families, as is the case with members of the Canadian seamen's union. During the process of fighting the war I saw many people in this house weeping salty tears for the Canadian merchant navy, the only part of our forces that fought the war under the banner of free enterprise. Why, if their wages were computed on an hourly basis, they were as low as sixteen cents an hour, working a twelve-hour day. Everyone spoke of the contribution they made, and that was all true. I think in proportion to number they suffered greater losses than any other branch of the service during the war.
I do not believe the other branches would have been able to fight the war but for the Canadian merchant marine. They would have starved to death but for them.
No one denies that.

The war is now over. The seamen were patient and long-suffering. They fought the war; they took their chances and did not interrupt shipping. The war is now over, and they have believed what we told them. I heard the Prime Minister say that we were fighting this war for a new philosophy

Supply-Labour Conditions
and a new order of society; that when this war was over, those who contributed or who offered their lives for their country were not going to come back to things which existed in pre-war years. Every last soldier, sailor and airman believed that sory. They accepted our word.
The Canadian seamen's union is not asking for much. They are asking for an 8-hour day, instead of the 12-hour day they are working, and for three watches on their ships. Then they want a little upward revision in their wages. Surely they earned that in the process of fighting the war. They were dealt out of everything. They did not have uniforms; they got a tin badge and that is all they got. Surely the least we can do is to protect them from thugs hired by private detective agencies. That sort of machinery should be outlawed, and that is why I rise to-night to bring this matter to the attention of the Minister of Justice. We went through all that thirty years ago.
Why, I could stand here for the next ten hours, and tell stories-

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. member has said that that was all they got. I want to say to him, on the authority of positive knowledge, that our merchant seamen of Canada got five times the benefits that merchant seamen of Great Britain got, as a result of the war.

You see, to compare this continent with Great Britain is below the intelligence of the minister. They are still getting their people out of air raid shelters in Great Britain; they are still depending upon this continent to feed them.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The merchant seamen saved England.
Yes, I concede that, and for England to get back on her feet again is still part of our job. But I like to get away sometimes from taking England as a yardstick.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Do not let us decry our own effort.

I am not doing that. What I said was that after a lot of struggle, for five years-and I am not blaming the minister for it, because I know he was as sympathetic as anybody in the house; but unfortunately he has that invisible treasury board to deal with-

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Not only that; he is a member of it.
Very likely a junior member.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: A senior member.
I can see the shadow of the Bank of Canada over him, and it frightens him.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No.

After a lot of pressure we did do some things for the merchant seamen. We restored benefits to -them, when they had no uniforms. Their incomes were taxed during most of the war-even their war risk bonus. They were never relieved of that, the taxation on war risk bonus; and they got back certain pension rights.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: But the hon. member said they got only a tin medal, and that is not right.
You do not see them going around wearing ribbons.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is not fair.
The only recognition they got for service-

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: They got 80 per cent of the benefits of the service men in the three fighting forces.
Yes, but still they have not the right to educational benefits, and things like that. I am expecting it will be 100 per cent before the veterans affairs committee finishes its work this session.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My hon. friend is always an optimist.

Well, it is just as well to be optimistic. When one loses hope, then it is time to get out of the picture.
As I was saying, however, I am strongly urging the Minister of Justice to examine into the activities of this detective agency, and into the organizing of thugs to break strikes.
I say that with a great deal of feeling, because I could tell the house many stories in connection with the establishment of unions in this country in the earlier days. In those days we met the same kind of people, many of them from the same city, evicting people from their homes, leaving them out on the sidewalk, chasing them out of town two or three times. I thought all that was finished at least fifteen years ago. It is unfortunate that we find it still existing in this province of Ontario, and allowed to exist in Quebec.
I am going to promise the minister that this is one question I will not forget. I shall continue to find out something about this until such time as we abolish illegal agencies of that kind in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. Earlier in the debate it was suggested that the member
Supply-Labour Conditions

for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) had quoted a wire without authority, owing to the fact that it was signed by one E. Dalskog in reply to a wire sent by B. G. Melsness.
My question of privilege is that another wire was handed to me three minutes ago. I particularly wish this to be put on the record, because it was implied that I was not speaking with authority or with correctness in respect of the wire I quoted, as coming from E. Dalskog, the international representative of I.W.A.
I wish now to quote the wire handed me:
Re letter following wire filed June 14 by E. Dalskog answering yours of 13th to me-
And this is the part which solves the fruit problem of British Columbia.
"-union prepared to immediately return men to work box factories under government controller with settlement of demands made with government after return to work." Letter following.
Who signed that?

Signed by B. G. Melsness. I wish now to conclude the matter of privilege. My responsibility as a member was questioned in respect of a wire I quoted and an answer I gave. I now wish to quote a letter from Mr. A. MacNamara, dated June 15, as follows:
The minister asked me to acknowledge receipt of copies of your correspondence with the international woodworkers association. I am sending copies to Hon. George Pearson and Hon. Mr. Justice Sloan by airmail.
"By airmail"-and we spent thousands of dollars in long distance calls. Then I am questioned as to whether I quoted correctly, and as to whether I had authority to speak for I.W.A. 1

On the request of the minister of labour of British Columbia I appointed Mr. Justice Sloan of the British Columbia appeal court to act as commissioner. In disputes of this kind one has to act with the principals, not with the fellows down in the trenches without any responsibility.
My hon. friend has quoted a wire from the organizer of that union. I may say that matter was checked. I am informed by Mr. Justice Sloan, in connection with the leader of the men's organization in British Columbia, and the terms indicated in the wire could not be carried out by the leader of the men's organization.
Motion agreed to, and the house went into committee of supply, Mr. Golding in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: As I indicated this afternoon, by agreement we are going to call two items which will be allowed to stand.

356. Departmental administration, $106,210.
Item stands.

369. Departmental administration, $199,115.
Item stands. -

National health branch-
223.	Advertising and labels division, $70,463.
The minister was to give us certain additional information on this item, particularly as compared with expenditures made in 1945-46.

speakeroldname: Hon. BROOKE CLAXTON (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
The leader of the opposition asked a question which I can best answer by telling the committee what happened. The work which is planned to be carried on by this advertising and labels division was carried on previously in part by the director of health services, by the food and drugs laboratory, by the laboratory on hygiene and by the proprietary or patent medicine division, four different divisions of the department's activities. It was found that the work was not being satisfactorily done because there was some overlapping. There were also some inconsistencies in the rulings made by departmental officers dealing either with radio advertising or with labelling. So it was decided, after the estimates for last year were prepared, to create a new division called the advertising and labels division.
This division was created on January 16, 1946, and an item of $13,000 was sought in the supplementary estimates to cover the expenses of the division for the remainder of the year. This item will be found on page 32 of the supplementary estimates. This vote represented the estimated expenses of the new division for the remaining three months of the year. It was not possible to set up the division before the end of the year, so that the amount actually expended was $100.11. The work of setting up the new division is proceeding and officers and employees from the old divisions are now being transferred. When the operation is completed the director of health services will not have anything to do with this operation except in an executive and administrative capacity. The food and drugs laboratory and the laboratory of hygiene will no longer have anything to do with this. The proprietary or patent medicine division will be absorbed and the new division will carry on the functions I described last Friday night.

Supply-Health, and Welfare
In view of the operation which I have just described and which is still under way, it is not possible to say how much of each of the previous expenses will be met out of this estimate. We are still engaged in forming this new division which will render better service to the trade, to advertisers and to the public of Canada. The amount sought here will be sufficient to carry on the work of the division after it has been set up, but as it is not by any means fully set up the amount will be prorated throughout the year and the full amount sought in this vote will not be expended. Because of lack of staff and space we have not been able to set up the positions which were created in the new division and the salaries for these will lapse. There will be no duplication of payment.

Item agreed to.
National health branch-[DOT]
224.	Grants to institutions assisting sailors, in the amounts detailed in the estimates, $2,400.

This vote covers grants of $200 each to twelve societies or organizations assisting sailors, but I wish to refer to only two, namely the Navy League of Canada at Halifax and the Navy League of Canada at Sydney. I am fairly familiar with the work that has been done by the navy league at all ports at which they have institutions, and in particular at. these two. I assume that this grant is merely a gesture of appreciation for the work that is done by those associated with the navy league. There is a long line of men and women in the communities across Canada who have given sincere and hard service to this work. They have been able to provide large sums of money, great quantities of clothing, many varieties of comforts, ditty bags and so forth for distribution to sailors. I know the minister must be familiar with the work, but I wonder if the country generally knows what was done by the Navy League of Canada during the last war?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I agree with everything the hon. member for Davenport has said.

Item agreed to.
National health branch-
225.	Medical services-Indians and Eskimos, $4,103,390.

It is not my intention to deal with this item at any length, because the matter of Indian affairs is before a special committee and I must be careful about any reference to that committee. There is an increase of over one and a half million dollars and I suppose the minister will have more complete details than are furnished' on page 63260-163
167 of the estimates. If this is to be used to provide medical services and so on for the Indians, I shall not oppose it.
Through many years I have visited about twenty-five Indian reservations, some in remote areas and others in the settled areas of Ontario, Quebec and Manitoba, so that I know something about this matter. Looking at page 167, I notice that three medical officers are being provided this year for the northwest territories. The next item shows an additional medical officer for the northwest territories. I have no doubt the minister will explain what these extra medical officers are going to do in that very large area. Last year there were thirty-two physicians, and this year there are thirty. That is going backward instead of forward. There were three graduate nurses last year, and1 two this year. The total medical service employees are fifty-six last year and fifty-six this year. There is an increase for temporary assistance of about $275,000 over last year. That would mean a lot of temporary assistance, and I hope the minister will explain what these additional temporary assistants are going to do.
There is a new item of $10,000 for publicity and information. I should like to know what that has to do with the Indian affairs branch. What does it want publicity for? It might have to do with instructing the Indians where to go for medical service, but I do not recollect any such item in any previous year. There was no such item last year. I notice that there is an increase of $5,000 for equipment maintenance and a considerable reduction in the item for acquisition of equipment. Is that equipment for hospitals for Indians? I am not opposed to reductions, but it is a large reduction and I had hoped that under the new minister the Indians would be getting a much better deal than ever before. There is a large increase in the item for construction of works and buildings. What is that for? Hospitals, schools or what? Another large item is for professional and special services. I presume that is for doctors, surgeons and nurses. Travelling expenses are up considerably, about $75,000. What does that large vote cover?
There will be another opportunity to discuss Indian affairs when the report from the Indian affairs committee comes before us. All I wish to say now is that I am anxious that a real change for the better will be made under these votes. I have long made up my mind, after consultation with teachers in the day schools on Indian reservations, particularly in remote areas such as around lake Nipigon, where you have to engage a boat

Supply-Health and Welfare

and go anywhere from twenty-five to fifty miles-I travelled over 100 miles by boat and paid $25 a day to make my own investigations -to bring this matter before the house. In one school I met a very bright teacher, and she strongly recommended-and I pass this on to the minister-that all teachers in the Indian schools be sent in their summer holidays by the department to some hospital or training school for thorough instruction in first aid. On one reservation I learned that the day before my visit an Indian had died just because there was no one present who could apply the most simple remedies for whatever sickness or illness he had. So I made up my mind that at the very first opportunity I would urge as strongly as I could that the teachers in the Indian schools in these remote areas like Fort Chipewyan, Fort Resolution, lake Nipigon and many other Indian reservations throughout the west-I met a very bright teacher at Fort a la Corne

be sent out at government expense and given a thorough training in first aid and applying the first remedies in all ordinary sicknesses until the Indian could be sent out for proper medical attention or a doctor brought in. This vote is largely for medical services and I am for anything that will improve the health of the Indians.
There is one other point. The Muncey reservation in Elgin county is a substantial Indian reservation, and if the minister had a talk with the doctor in charge-I do not know whether it is the same man now-the doctor would tell him one thing, and that is that if the Muncey reservation had a hospital like the one at Oshweken on the Six Nations reserve, it would be of great benefit to the Indians. The great trouble in getting the Indians to go to hospital some distance away is that the love of the Indian father and mother for their children is so great that they cannot bear to see one of them go away to a hospital at London, Chatham, Windsor or Woodstock. Much better results would be obtained if there were a small hospital on the Muncey reservation, and then the Indians would not have to send their children a considerable distance away to hospital. The department has a first-class doctor at Muncey, perhaps more than one. At least the man I met was excellent and very sympathetic. I have the highest opinion of him. He may not be there now because I met him some years ago.
I leave these two suggestions with the minister, that a small hospital be put up for the Indians where there is a substantial reserva-

tion, and, second, that the teachers in Indian schools in the remote areas be given thorough instruction in first aid.

The hon. member for Davenport has pretty well covered the ground with respect to the Indians, and I endorse what he has said. I am pleased to see an increase in the estimates for medical services to the Indians and Eskimos. If the money is properly spent-and I hope it will be-great good can come therefrom. I propose to address myself now to the problems of the Eskimos.
We know that the Eskimos are badly in need of medical and dental care, care for their eyes and so on. I understand that each year medical services are made available on the Nascopie, which travels to the far north. A medical doctor and a dentist provide inspection, care and corrective treatment for the Eskimos who present themselves on the boat during the time it is being unloaded. Coming from the war expenditures committee I have heard reports that boats are being sold at a very small sum compared with the original cost. I am not mentioning this by way of criticism because it is not my intention to go into that at the moment. My purpose is to recommend to the minister that his department give consideration to acquiring a suitable vessel from the Department of Munitions and Supply or War Assets Corporation with a view to equipping it as a hospital ship to be devoted largely to the health and welfare problems of the Eskimos, who would then not have to depend entirely upon the Hudson's Bay company boat which puts in at northern ports for a limited time while it is unloading. In other words, I am suggesting that the department give more particular attention to providing better services to the Eskimos, and I am suggesting, as a means to that end, that it acquire a suitable vessel, properly equipped as a hospital ship, and send it on its voyage so that it can play an adequate part in the health and welfare and general advancement of the Eskimos, for whose care we are largely responsible. That is about the only observation I have to make, along with my endorsa-tion of what the hon. member for Davenport has said with respect to our Indians.

I should like to take the minister back to Manitoba for the time being. I have a great number of Indians in my constituency. I do not rise in a critical mood, but I want to be sure that the services of the Department of Mines and Resources and of the minister's own department are not duplicated. I am going to take him to Norway House and ask him to consider the position

Supply-Health and Welfare
of an Indian there with tuberculosis. I want him to tell me what is done. Has he a superintendent of medical services for Indians, in Winnipeg? If the minister can answer me as I go along it may save time.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: At Norway House there is a resident full-time doctor.
When Doctor Corrigan at Norway House decides that a patient must have treatment in a hospital, what is the next step?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Move him to the nearest general hospital.

How are you going to move
him?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: If necessary, by air.
Who is going to sanction air transportation?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: We usually do it here in Ottawa.
You do not mean to tell me that somebody is lying dying at Norway House, 425 miles north of Winnipeg, and you have to come to Ottawa to ask for sanction to move a dying patient?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: The hon. member is just a shade ahead of us. We are planning the appointment of eight regional superintendents who will include that as their responsibility and duty.
I asked you if you had one at Winnipeg.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Not yet. We are setting up these posts.

There will be one at Winnipeg? Well, then, what is the Indian agent going to do, if your doctor does him out of his job? You cannot employ a highly paid doctor to do the work of an Indian agent. Doctors are more valuable to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I do not know whether the hon. member is in favour of our having more doctors or less.
I am in favour of having more doctors.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
We have a resident fulltime doctor at Norway House; we propose to have a regional superintendent at Winnipeg; and they will not compete with the Indian agent in any sense whatever. They will work very closely with him. If the Indian agent receives word of anyone being ill he will tell the nearest doctor. If he cannot reach 63260-163i
a doctor he will get out word by radio if he has that equipment, and we will take the necessary action.
Do you intend to have an aeroplane of your own for moving these people?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: An air ambulance?
An air ambulance.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: We have not any, but we have been immensely assisted during the war, as I believe the hon. member knows from the statement I made in the Indian affairs committee-I think he was there-by the assistance given us by the Royal Canadian Air Force and the United States Army Air Force, both of which had . extensive establishments in the north country. That will now be replaced either by Royal Canadian Air Force assistance or by our hiring, as we frequently do, privately owned planes or else borrowing an R.C.A.F. or Department of Transport plane. We do not at present propose to have a private air force of our own. The territory is so great that it would take a considerable number of planes to cover it. It would not be an economic way to use planes; they would not be in the air a sufficient portion of the time to be economically used. What we aim to do is to use by one means or another the resources there are, and when we get stuck we shall find some other way of doing it.

At the present time, if anyone takes sick at Norway House and is brought to Winnipeg, will your branch be responsible for the movement from the train to the hospital, or will that be done by the Indian agent in Winnipeg?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: As far as the patient's health is concerned we are responsible for that.
But it is not only the supervision of his health, but transportation, and everything-*

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Everything in relation to his health will be attended to by us.
You have to make that plainer for me. I want to understand this thoroughly before I leave it.
Order. I ask the hon. member to address the Chair.

I am sorry, Mr. Chairman I will try not to hurt your feelings any more. Mr. Chairman, I want to carry this farther; I want to get to the bottom of it,
Supply-Health and Welfare

because I know the trouble the Indians have had in coming from these places-Norway House, Grand Rapids, Berens River-they are three or four days on the way. Somebody must be responsible for them. When Doctor Corrigan puts them on the boat his duties are ended. Does the minister intend to increase that service by having somebody to look after them on the boat, or is there to be an Indian agent to do it?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I have already answered the hon. gentleman. In so far as the health of the Indians is concerned this department is responsible, and if an Indian is to be moved for reasons of health this department will be responsible.

There are so many
Indians at Norway House, Berens River and Grand Rapids that I suggest the minister follow the same plan he did at Oshweken, as far as he can, and put up a small hospital there.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: We have a hospital there. We aim, as part of the programme of construction, to replace that with a larger and fire-resistant hospital.
At Nonvay House?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Yes. Also to have a
number of nursing stations in that area, which has a total Indian population in that agency of 3,740.
Where is the hospital now?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: At Norway House.
I thought there was a hospital there, and I wondered why my hon. friend was speaking about the necessity of taking patients away from Norway House.

I should like the hon. member for Davenport to know that it is only a twelve-bed hospital; we have people dying there with tuberculosis, dying like flies, and they have to be moved to the new hospital at The Pas. Can the minister tell the committee what progress has been made with the hospital at The Pas; how many beds it contains; who has been appointed as doctor there, and give other information about it?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
At The Pas there is the Clearwater Lake Indian hospital, which was taken over from the United States army. It is a 100-bed hospital, and it is planned to enlarge that hospital quite considerably so as to make a more efficient use of the large central equipment they have. The number of beds will then be increased considerably.

speechtext: It would depend on the situation. If the patient is in an acute or very infectious stage he would be put there for a time until he could be moved somewhere else. Certainly a hospital of that kind is not suitable for the care and cure of tuberculosis. It has twenty-two beds.

I should like the
minister to give us a breakdown of this large amount. How much of it is for hospitals; how much for doctors who devote their full time to the work and how much for doctors who devote part of their time? I know that in some provinces some of the reservations, such as those in Saskatchewan for instance, are some distance away from doctors. That may still be true. I know for a fact that sometimes the doctor makes a visit to treat an Indian who suffers perhaps from eye trouble and the bill amounts to about $25. Is there a maximum charge which the doctor can make? The doctors used to charge so much a mile, and then so much for the visit. Is that the system in vogue at the present time? If so, then the question arises as to whether the reservation should not have a doctor, or whether the doctor should not live closer to it, or whether some other means could be found to keep down what seems to be a large expense.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Perhaps I should answer the various questions raised by the hon. member for Davenport and other hon. members. As has been said, the increase now being sought from the figure of $2,526,000 to $4,103,390, an increase of $1,577,390, is a substantial increase. That is sought because we are determined to take positive steps about the health of the Indians and Eskimos of Canada. The plans were made by the Indian affairs branch of the Department of Mines and Resources before the Indian health services were transferred to this department, to take effect from November 1, 1945. Since then we have gone over them carefully with the advantage of having direct contact between the Indian affairs doctors and our own doctors; we have drawn up a programme for Indian health services which hon. members who are interested will find summarized at page 75 of the proceeding of the special joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons, appointed to examine and consider the Indian Act, when I made a submission on June 6, 1946. The proposals of the programme of the department for the Indian health services are summarized there, and hon. members will see throughout the proceedings information which would answer many of the questions asked here.
One of the questions related to the general scope of the increased services proposed. These
include greatly improved health services to Eskimos, opening three hospitals in the current fiscal year with a total bed capacity of 650, increasing by more than fifty per cent the departmental hospital bed capacity. These additions are the Miller Bay near Prince Rupert, taken over from the air force about a year ago with 150 beds, the Edmonton Indian hospital taken over from the army about November 1, 1945, with 400 beds, of which at least 100, with 100 more temporarily, are earmarked for veterans so long as they need them, the Clearwater Lake Indian hospital taken over from the United States army, 100 beds. The programme also provides for more adequate health services, and consequently the treatment of many more patients.
The hon. member for Davenport asked about the considerable increase in the amount sought for professional services, and that was referred to by another hon. member. This amount covers the expenditure by the department on part-time doctors. These doctors are engaged on various bases, depending on the local circumstances. Some of them are paid on a fee per patient basis; others at an amount per month. Altogether I can assure my hon. friends that the amounts paid are not regarded either by the department or by doctors as excessive. Their accounts are submitted in detail. They are gone over and, after verification, are paid according to the scales which have been established. I am sure that in some respects the amounts paid are not in line with the amounts paid for medical services rendered to other patients in the same area.
Are they higher or lower?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
They are lower. On the other hand, in ordinary times it does provide a steady source of income for doctors; but at the present time when doctors are overworked it is not quite as attractive as it used to be.
In addition to the departmental hospitals, Indians are hospitalized in general hospitals. During 1945, 16,239 Indians were hospitalized outside departmental hospitals for a total of 404,730 days in 417 hospitals. We intend to render more hospital service.
Reference has been made to tuberculosis, and the incidence of tuberculosis among Indians and Eskimos is very much greater than that among the white population.
About seventeen times as great.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
On the average the figures are fifteen times as great as for the white population of Canada. They vary from place to place. In places like the Mohawk, the Six
Supply-Health and Welfare

Nations reserve, they are three times as great. But there are localities in which it is even greater than fifteen times as great as among the white population. That presents a special problem of diagnosis, isolation, treatment and cure. As we know, tuberculosis is a disease which can be cured. We have reduced the tuberculosis mortality among the white population from something like 200 per 100,000 at the beginning of the century to something in the neighbourhood of 45 per 100,000 to-day. In other words, among the whites we have wiped out three-quarters of the killing power of tuberculosis. That is not the case with the Indians; and in order to tackle that job we require a considerable increase in hospital beds, in X-ray equipment for diagnosis, and so on. This plan we have under way aims at achieving as much as we can do with the staff and space and facilities we can expect to get during the next year. In other words, this year money is not a limiting factor. The limitations on the service will be those of securing adequate, experienced staff and being able to do the amount of construction we aim to do. The results will not be immediately spectacular, because tuberculosis and other conditions of this kind cannot be dealt with in a year; but with a determined effort and a long-term programme there is no doubt at all but that we can substantially improve the health of the Indians. The building programme for this year includes a new hospital at Moose Factory which we hope to begin-

Is that to be built out on Moose island or on the mainland at Moosonee?
Mr. CLAXTON; My understanding is that it will be on the mainland, but I shall verify that- and give the bon. member the information later. At Fort Qu'Appelle, Saskatchewan, there is to be a fifty-bed extension to the present hospital; also a building replacing a nurses' home destroyed by fire; provision of adequate power house and doctor's residence. At Coqualeetza Indian hospital at Sardis, British Columbia, we are to build a nurses' home, power house, doctor's residence and children's ward. At the Edmonton hospital, Edmonton, we hope to do the necessary alterations and complete the building. Then at the Clearwater Lake Indian hospital, Le Pas, Manitoba, we are to build a doctor's residence. We also aim at least to commence the construction of five additional nursing stations at Bersimis, Quebec; Eskasoni, B.C.; Fort George, Quebec; Gypsumville, Manitoba, and St. Regis, Quebec.

The hon. member for Davenport also asked the reason for an item of $10,000 for publicity and information. That is designed to begin an educational programme among the Indians and Eskimos. There, as elsewhere, we find the greatest obstacle to health is ignorance and failure to put into practice what we know we can do. This programme involves the preparation of two simple leaflets in colour on child care and the rules of hygiene; the purchase of some pamphlets for use in hospitals; some simple, colourful posters; a film strip; a motion picture news clip, and then the translation of these into the Cree syllabics. This will account for this expenditure. In answer to earlier questions I should say that the hospital at Moose Factory will be on Moose island. The Clearwater Lake hospital at Le Pas, to which the hon. member for Selkirk referred, is about one hundred miles from Norway House by plane. I should add that the local doctor has authority, in the event of an emergency case and it being impossible to deal with the matter in any other way or to refer it to Ottawa, to take the responsibility upon himself of getting a plane.
One hundred miles from where?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: From Norway House.

There must be some mistake. Even by air it is 110 miles from the Pas to Cedar Lake, and it is thirty-six miles across the lake and then twenty miles from the lake to Grand Rapids; then from The Pas across to Norway House is a trip requiring a whole night and a morning by boat. I should say it would be 150 to 200 miles if it is a mile.

I should like to ask another question on that. The Norway House residential school was destroyed by fire a couple of weeks ago. Has the minister any information as to the data and information collected at that school concerning vitamins and nutrition? I am sure he is aware of the manner in which the school was divided into four sections and, how they all got different biscuits so many times a day or so many times week. Does the minister know if the material they were able to build up in that study has been destroyed?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I have the report on that nutritional survey in my hand at the moment. It was completed.

I think it would be interesting to mention it to the committee. It was good work.

Supply-Health and Welfare

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: It is exceedingly useful work. This survey of nutrition among North American Indians was conducted by the acting superintendent of the medical service, Doctor P. E. Moore and by Doctor F. F. Tisdall, who is very well known and who was consultant to the armed forces, as well as by the local doctor, Doctor R. S. C. Corrigan, and by Doctor Kruse of the Millbank memorial fund of New York. They obtained valuable results, which are being used not only in connection with health services to the Indians and Eskimos but also in connection with family allowances to the Indians and Eskimos in kind.
My question was really about the records in the school. Do you know if they were destroyed?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I do not know.

We have two Indian reserves in Bruce county, and I am glad to say they are among the healthier reserves which were mentioned by the minister a few moments ago. The fact is, however, that we are still short of hospitals in Bruce, and we are having two built, one very close to the Cape Croker reserve and the other close to the Saugeen reserve. These hospitals are being built largely by public subscription, and I should like to ask the minister if his department would consider helping out with. a donation, large or small as they may see fit, in order to help in the hospitalization of these Indians.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: We would have to know the circumstances of the case. In a limited number of cases grants have been made to hospitals, but only where the Indians in the locality represented a very large proportion of the population and the services necessary for the Indians could not be provided more economically in any other way, or as part of the regular services of the hospital. We have had many applications, and I had occasion to mention this two weeks ago, when the matter came up. We have had applications from every part of Canada; but, as hon. members know, hospitalization ordinarily is a matter for the provinces. In the great majority of cases the Indian health "service pays the daily cost of hospitalizing an Indian as its contribution, in accordance with arrangements worked out with each hospital. Ordinarily we do not make capital grants.

Would the minister give consideration to taking over the American army hospital at Churchill? I visited there in 1943, at which time there were seven American doctors at that point. Frequently they were called out in emergencies to some of
the Indian settlements and also to attend the Eskimos, and they were greatly concerned about the type of medical service we were providing in that area. In view of the fact that the supply situation is to be a factor, and since I understand that this establishment has been taken over by the Canadian government, it seems a pity not to make use of it. I can think of no good reason why the minister should not use these facilities for the benefit of the Eskimos and Indians in that north country. Could the minister state whether this has been given any consideration?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I can state in a general way that consideration has been given to the taking over of every hospital occupied by the navy, army or air force of Canada or of the United States in Canada. We have looked at every situation, and a great number of them are still receiving consideration, so I shall be very glad to see that this is looked into further.

I note that the amount for temporary assistance under this vote has increased by almost $300,000. Does that include professional assistance or non-professional? If it is professional, why is it not included under the item for professional and special services which appears farther down in the list? It seems to me it must represent *. change in policy, when we find such a considerable change in the amount of the item. I notice further that the item for cash allowances is more than doubled, going from $21,000 to $90,000. What is the nature of those allowances?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
An item for temporary assistance appears in the votes of almost every department. That item covers salaries or wages of personnel whose positions have not yet been made permanent, but who may continue in service for some time. In this instance it includes a considerable increase in professional personnel, owing to the fact that we have taken over the hospitals I mentioned, with a bed capacity of 650.
We propose, too, to have eight regional superintendents, including one from Manitoba and western Ontario. It also includes the addition of a considerable number of nurses for nursing stations, as soon as we can get them.
What about cash allowances?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I shall answer that a little later on, if that is satisfactory to the hon. member.

What is the infant mortality rate among Eskimos and Indians? Are those separated from the general rates for all Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
The infant mortality rate among Indians is given at page 91 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the special joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons on the Indian Act. I should make it clear that they are there given under the heading of diseases peculiar to the first year of life, and the rates are set out per 100,000 of population.
Infant mortality rates are usually sho<wn per 1,000 of live births. Here, however, the figures on the number of live births are not reliable, with the result that the figure given is a rate peir 100,000 of papulation. It will be seen that the rates for 1942, 1943, and 1944 are, roughly, three times as high as the white rate for all Canada, exclusive of the northwest territories. However, we do not know accurately the number of live births. So that if there is a greater proportion of births imong the Indians and Eskimos than there is among the rest of the population, the infant mortality rate per 1,000 live births will be relatively smaller than shown here. However, as shown here it is three times as high as the whites.
Is any clinical or pre-natal care taken, or any attempt made to reduce the rate?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: In the Six Nations reserve, where there are 6,600 Indians, I believe every baby is born in a hospital, and the rate compares favourably with that among the white population. In other localities every possible assistance is given, in relation to the possibilities in those localities. There are only nine doctors in the whole of the northwest territories and the Arctic, but we hope to establish more doctors and more nursing centres to supplement the doctors. We also hope to do much more by way of education among the Indians, and also by way of special training of traders, factors, members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and others in the north, including missionaries and teachers, so that they will be able to give more than just first aid assistance.

Can the minister tell the committee in what percentage of reserves across Canada are nursing stations with well-equipped dispensaries? I am of opinion that we have a large number of small reserves located at great distances from hospitals. Those reserves are visited rarely by Indian agents, and I am wondering what such people will do in the future. Will nurses be

stationed at such points to help them in their health difficulties, or does the department plan any extension work to place nurses on such reserves, so as to administer to the needs of the people before they have to go to hospital? I am referring particularly to the north Pacific coast.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Every band of Indians in Canada has been surveyed. We have drawn up a long-term plan which provides by one means or another for their securing adequate health services. This plan has to be developed as people become available to carry it out, and as we develop the technical and administrative experience requisite to enable us to handle it. But every band-in fact, every group of Indians across Canada-is plotted on this map, and we aim by one means or another, where they have not existing services, to provide them with adequate health services.

I did not hear the minister's comment replying to the suggestion for a special hospital ship for the far north, and I therefore wish to address a further question in that connection. Does the minister consider the facilities of the Hudson bay boat adequate to meet the demands of this trip? I understand that the quarters are cramped, and that the facilities can be considered only as makeshift. What is the feasibility of the department's owning a ship which could be properly equipepd as a hospital ship? Does the minister consider the facilities of the Hudson bay vessel adequate?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I believe I overlooked
answering that part of the hon. member's question. We have looked into the matter of providing a special hospital ship. My recollection is that the cost of such a vessel would be about $250,000. This vessel would have had to be taken over from War Assets Corporation, and reconstructed. The amount I have mentioned would be largely the cost of putting it into shape for a northern, voyage. The annual cost of operation would be something like $25,000. The effective period during which it would be in the far north where it would be useful would be. somewhere betwen six and ten weeks, depending on the season. It would be an extremely expensive operation.
As I say, we have considered the matter, and still have it under consideration. But it would seem to us that that is not the most effective and economical way of doing the job.
As to the hon. member's further question concerning the adequacy of the services provided by the Nascopie, let me say that we are extremely glad to have those services. As hon. members are aware, the ship carries two doctors-usually most distinguished ones-who

Supply-Health and Welfare
render service during that trip. Relief doctors and nurses are also sent up. It would be much better if the ship could stay longer at each port of call, but primarily its visits are not for reasons of health but to provide service for the Hudson's Bay company and the other people who are on it. However, it does a very useful work and we are glad) to have it. My hope would be that if the Hudson's Bay company are planning to replace the Nascopie they will do it with a larger vessel which would permit us to provide greater services on board.
Are trained Indian nurses going to New Zealand to take courses in midwifery?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I did not know of that.
The minister has not answered the question asked by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard in connection with cash allowances, $90,580.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Those are paid as maintenance to professional people and others who live away from the hospital or the nursing station to compensate for board and lodging.
It is a living allowance to people on the regular staff?

speechtext: Yes.

Would the minister
explain the increase from $21,360 to $90,580?

It is hardly likely you will require this amount this year. The minister can hardly expect to get all this hospital development under way.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That would be the target. We shall not get the number of nurses and professional help to use the full amount the way things are going.

The minister has given considerable detail in connection with the item for construction of works and buildings, but I do not think we have had a summing up. What is the cost per bed of this type of hospital construction given in terms that we can compare with hospital construction elsewhere? What bed accommodation is expected to be provided out of this item of $840,000?

speechtext:
I am afraid I have not it broken down in that way. The cost per bed in most of these hospitals is much less than the cost of general hospital construction in cities after you have provided for transporting the materials. You can imagine that the cost of transporting materials, workmen and equipment to do a job at Moose Factory would add enormously to the cost, but actu-63260-164
ally the cost of this type of hospital construction is much less than that of general hospital construction in the larger cities.
What will be the total hospital bed accommodation provided by this item of $840,000?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: It will be in the neighbourhood of 200 beds.

I should like to pursue the question raised a while ago by the hon. member for Selkirk about the lack of medical care on the Indian reserves. I understood the minister to say that the medical care of Indians has been transferred to his department from Mines and Resources. Who is responsible for reporting cases of tuberculosis or other diseases found on the reserves? I suppose the Indian agent would still be under the Department of Mines and Resources, but medical care of the Indians is now under the Department of National Health and Welfare. Where do the two tie up? Does anyone take the initiative in reporting cases of disease on the reserve, or does the department depend upon the provincial health and welfare departments who send public health nurses around to the schools? What system is used?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: There is no difference at all in reporting cases from what it was before, except that we hope to have a larger personnel in the field. We hope to have more trained dispensers and a closer tie-in with the provincial authorities. Apart from that, the Indian agent, the doctor, the nurse or the provincial representative report the cases just as before. There is no division to prevent the Indian agent from communicating directly with us; in fact in some places the Indian agent is the same person as the Indian health sendee doctor.

To what extent is there cooperation between the provincial health departments and the Department of National Health and Welfare? Is any use made of the reports submitted by the provincial public health nurses who visit the schools on the Indian reserves? There is a lot of data and information obtained in that way that could be used by the department if it were channeled into the department. Is there any liaison there?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Yes. On the Six Nations reserve we are undertaking a mass survey of all the Indians for tuberculosis. They are to be X-rayed in July and August by arrangement with the provincial health authorities. Close cooperation with the provincial authorities obtains right across Canada.

Indian nurses. That is usually provided by the bands or the Indian affairs branch, but we will certainly look into the question of facilitating that training.

Would the minister give figures indicating the incidence of venereal disease within, say the last two years, to establish trends, including both the civilian population and the armed services?

With respect to this item of $4,000, I wonder again where it really fits into the picture. The welfare branch consists of the family allowances division, which has its own and a quite large publicity vote, the old age pensions and pensions for the blind division, and the national physical fitness division, which again has its own item for publicity. I said, when I first raised this question about publicity, . that I was sure the minister could give some reason why each one of these publicity or educational items should be in the estimates. Naturally the members have to rely to a great extent upon the discretion of the minister, but I think it would be appropriate for me to say here that, as we have gone through the various items, I have not seen any general coordination of these quite large sums of money, totalling over $500,000, which would lead me to be certain that the money was being spent in the right place for the most useful purposes. It has been my impression, from the answers the minister has given, that the items are usually made up upon separate requests from provincial organizations or from the dominion health council which the officers of the department have met, and which have all seemed perfectly right and proper and been approved by the departmental officials and then have appeared in the estimates. We are dealing here with something which is nebulous and the value of which cannot be gauged as easily as the value of a doctor's services or the expenditure of a certain amount on drugs. I should very much like to see that this money was spent according to certain general principles laid down by the minister, in order that the money may be well spent. It would seem to me, although I am an absolute amateur at the game, that were I in the minister's position I should like to see this $500,000 spent perhaps in five large chunks for five specific services this year, so that at the end of the year I could tell whether the story I had to tell had definitely got over to the Canadian people in each of these five directions. Then next year perhaps take five other services. That is only my opinion. I would urge that the minister work out an over-all policy for publicity and educational expenses which will satisfy him, because he is the person who must be responsible to the house for the efficacy of his expenditures, that
he is really getting over to the Canadian people the picture he wants, rather than a hundred little pictures which are requested by a hundred different agents.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I appreciate the hon. member's comment. It seems to me that he is now contradicting one of the principles which he laid down when he first spoke on this subject. He said he thought one of the first principles should be that the publicity be directed to some particular group to which it was suited and from which it was hoped to obtain definite response. That is something we have had in mind with regard to publicity generally, but not in connection with family allowance publicity because there, since we deal with the parents of 92 per cent of the population, we deal with virtually everyone.
I should like to quote in this connection an interesting' comment on this discussion, when it occurred last, from the Winnipeg Tribune for June 3, in which it is said:
Health and welfare is an important concern of the Canadian people, educational work on a large scale is essential to it, and the colonel might well be asked what other department has in his judgment a better right to stand second to trade and commerce in its publicity appropriations.
Colonel Merritt conceded that booklets dealing with child and maternal care were a good investment. He has perhaps heard-since the opinion is universally held by parents who have made use of these booklets-that they are of unrivalled excellence. But he apparently does not know that these booklets are distributed by and through the provincial departments of health "who have trained staffs in the field." Far from "by-passing" the provincial departments, as the colonel charged, the national department works in close and constant cooperation with them at every point where such cooperation is feasible.
"Telling people what to eat on picnics" may seem an absurdity to Colonel Merritt, but the fact is that the department's manual on camp feeding is a model of its kind-
Will the minister permit an interruption? Is he not offending against a well-known rule of the house by reading editorials here?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: No.
I am not asking the minister's point of view on it. I should like to know the views of the Chairman, because he is the one who rules the house.
I should like to say-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I should just like to finish this, if I may:

and meets a real need in an important sector of the nutrition field.

One moment, please. I know the minister rules the department, but he does not rule the committee-yet. Perhaps the Chairman would give a ruling on the
Supply-Health and Welfare

question I raised, because many of us have been stopped before, and I hope there is not one rule for the rich and one for the poor.
It is something which should not be done. I hope the hon. member will see to it that the rule is observed, and I would ask the minister also to observe it.

May I say that it is not my purpose and never was my purpose to criticize proper expenditures on education, and if any newspapers in the country have a different view I suppose I cannot correct them, but I do not think the minister and I have any misapprehension as to what I have said throughout this debate. I simply indicated to him- and I thought this was the appropriate time- that one member of this committee does not feel satisfied that there is a proper over-all policy in regard to these expenditures, and I merely asked him if he would take that in consideration in his department for the next estimates.

Would the minister care to
comment on the matter of the supply or lack of supply of trained case workers for family welfare work? Theirs is a work which requires a particular type of individual and an intensive and specific training. Has the minister considered granting, say national scholarships to encourage young people to go into this work, because unless I am wrongly informed there is a sad dearth of people able to carry it on in the proper manner?

speechtext: Item 232, which we shall come to, provides $100,000 expressly for that purpose.

Surely they come under item 228.

I wish to discuss the question of old age pensions.

There was a good deal of information which I was going to ask the minister for. If I indicate it now, it may give him

an opportunity to muster the information and make it available to the committee at the next sitting.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I may say that, in view of the fact that this month we complete almost a year of family allowance administration, I thought the committee and others would be interested in a fairly complete statement with the filing of figures showing eleven full months of administration and some general observations on the way it has worked out, and I am prepared to do that just as soon as we get another opportunity. I think some of the hon. member's questions would be anticipated in the statement I intended to make.

Would it assist the minister if I indicated now, in just a word or two, the points I think might be covered? In the first place, we had, on December 15, 1945, shown on pages 3603 and 3604 of Hansard, certain tables. Would the minister bring down comparable tables for the last month for which figures are available?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: They will be filed right up to May.
In the item of $150,000 for publicity and information could we have the expenditures and the projected plan?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Yes.
In the next place, the expenditures contracted for by months to date from the commencement of the operation of the family allowances, in respect of publicity.
Does the minister wish to put the tables on Hansard?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: If I might, I should like to file,, first, a table showing family allowance payments for the months from July, 1945, when the first payment was made, to May, 1946, when the last payment was made; second, a table showing statistics based on the May, 1946, family allowances payments; and, third, further statistics, broken down by provinces, of the payments in May, 1946. May I have the unanimous consent of the committee to put this on Hansard? We have some further tables to be filed later, but it will, I hope, be a convenience to hon. members if I file these now.
Agreed.
